<section id="S3.SS2.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.2.1 </span>Unified Pretraining of Continuous and Discrete dLMs</h4>

<section id="S3.SS2.SSS1.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Data.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS1.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS1.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As with NLD, we adopt the open-sourced pretraining data from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Basant et al. (2025)</a></cite>. We use the Mistral-NeMo tokenizer (<math id="S3.SS2.SSS1.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V=131{,}072" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>V</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>131,072</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V=131{,}072</annotation></semantics></math>)  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib66" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mistral AI, 2024</a>)</cite>, batch size <math id="S3.SS2.SSS1.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="512" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>512</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">512</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S3.SS2.SSS1.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L=4096" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4096</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L=4096</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS1.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Architecture.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS1.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS1.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.SSS1.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span> adopts the transformer backbone of NLD and its AR baseline, ensuring the three families are parameter- and FLOP-matched. As with NLD, <span id="S3.SS2.SSS1.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span> uses a block causal attention mask (<a href="#S3.F2.sf2" title="In Figure 2 ‣ 3 Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2(b)</span></a>). <span id="S3.SS2.SSS1.Px2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span> uniquely adds a unit-norm 16-dimensional diffusion embedding table with a linear up-projection, a categorical reparameterization mapping <math id="S3.SS2.SSS1.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>V</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V</annotation></semantics></math>-dimensional probabilities to low-dimensional soft embeddings, a self-conditioning linear projection, Fourier time conditioning, and a learnable noise schedule (see <a href="#S2" title="2 Background ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>). Together, these account for less than <math id="S3.SS2.SSS1.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1\%</annotation></semantics></math> of the total parameters. We provide thorough details in <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Implementation Details and Additional Results for Pretraining ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">App.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS1.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Training.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS1.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS1.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We train our models for 150k steps, following the optimization procedure detailed in <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Implementation Details and Additional Results for Pretraining ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">App.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a>. Given a batch size of 512, 150k steps correspond to over 300B tokens. Training consumed <math id="S3.SS2.SSS1.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim\!9{,}600" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>∼</mo><mn>9,600</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim\!9{,}600</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS2.SSS1.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim\!19{,}200" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>∼</mo><mn>19,200</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim\!19{,}200</annotation></semantics></math> NVIDIA GB200 GPU hours for the 3B and 8B models, respectively.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.2.2 </span>AR Initialization and Regularization</h4>

<section id="S3.SS2.SSS2.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">AR Initialization.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS2.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS2.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To evaluate the impact of initialization, we compare pretraining <span id="S3.SS2.SSS2.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span> (<span id="S3.SS2.SSS2.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">i</span>) from scratch and (<span id="S3.SS2.SSS2.Px1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">ii</span>) from an AR baseline pretrained on 1T tokens. Due to the dimension mismatch between high-dimensional AR embeddings and <span id="S3.SS2.SSS2.Px1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span>’s 16-dimensional space, we randomly initialize the diffusion embedding layer. As shown in <a href="#S3.F3.sf1" title="In Figure 3 ‣ 3.2 Pretraining ‣ 3 Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figs.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3(a)</span></a> and <a href="#S3.F3.sf2" title="Figure 3(b) ‣ Figure 3 ‣ 3.2 Pretraining ‣ 3 Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3(b)</span></a>, <span id="S3.SS2.SSS2.Px1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span> -<span id="S3.SS2.SSS2.Px1.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">unreg</span>-3B (<math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L^{\prime}=64" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>L</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>64</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L^{\prime}=64</annotation></semantics></math>) with self-conditioning achieves competitive perplexity relative to NLD-3B (<math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L^{\prime}=64" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>L</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>64</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L^{\prime}=64</annotation></semantics></math>) under both regimes (<span id="S3.SS2.SSS2.Px1.p1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">i</span>) and (<span id="S3.SS2.SSS2.Px1.p1.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">ii</span>). However, AR initialization significantly accelerates convergence and yields lower final training loss.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS2.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">AR Regularization.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS2.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS2.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Continuous diffusion training inherently suffers from high gradient variance and slow convergence. To mitigate variance and accelerate optimization, we follow NLD by adding AR regularization, optimizing the joint objective <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\text{ar}}+w_{\text{diff}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{BD}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>ar</mtext></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mtext>diff</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>BD</mtext></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\text{ar}}+w_{\text{diff}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{BD}}</annotation></semantics></math> (<a href="#S3.F3.sf3" title="In Figure 3 ‣ 3.2 Pretraining ‣ 3 Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3(c)</span></a>; see <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Implementation Details and Additional Results for Pretraining ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">App.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a> for the <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{\text{diff}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>w</mi><mtext>diff</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{\text{diff}}</annotation></semantics></math> weighting schedule), where</p>
<table id="S3.E6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E6.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\text{ar}}={\textstyle\sum}_{l=2}^{L}-\log\langle{\mathbf{x}}_{\theta}^{l}({\mathbf{x}}^{&lt;l}),{\mathbf{x}}^{l}\rangle" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>ar</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="false"><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mi>L</mi></msubsup></mstyle><mo>−</mo><mi>log</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟨</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>θ</mi><mi>l</mi></msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>l</mi></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">⟩</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\text{ar}}={\textstyle\sum}_{l=2}^{L}-\log\langle{\mathbf{x}}_{\theta}^{l}({\mathbf{x}}^{&lt;l}),{\mathbf{x}}^{l}\rangle</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(6)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS2.Px2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">is computed over the AR stream using causal attention (<a href="#S3.F2" title="In 3 Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>). This architecture employs two distinct readout heads, with the AR regularization computed exclusively from the AR head. While this dual-head formulation improves auxiliary AR decoding capability, our primary objective remains maximizing diffusion decoding performance.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS2.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS2.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Finally, input sequences utilize AR embeddings for the AR stream and 16-dimensional diffusion embeddings for the diffusion stream (<a href="#S3.F2" title="In 3 Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>), facilitating AR initialization and efficient KV-caching. As shown in <a href="#S3.F3.sf3" title="In Figure 3 ‣ 3.2 Pretraining ‣ 3 Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3(c)</span></a>, AR regularization significantly improves training stability; with a properly tuned <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.Px2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{\text{diff}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>w</mi><mtext>diff</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{\text{diff}}</annotation></semantics></math>, it even outperforms pure perplexity optimization for the diffusion stream. This confirms that AR regularization stabilizes training while yielding a higher-quality model. Consequently, we adopt AR initialization, AR regularization, and a block size of <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.Px2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L^{\prime}=32" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>L</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>32</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L^{\prime}=32</annotation></semantics></math> for all subsequent <span id="S3.SS2.SSS2.Px2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span> experiments.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Language Generation via Continuous Diffusion Sampling</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Drawing on the success of continuous diffusion samplers using SDE/ODE solvers <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Song et al., 2021b</a>)</cite>, we systematically explore decoding samplers for continuous dLMs, evaluating performance across standard mathematical reasoning and coding benchmarks.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Block Diffusion Sampling</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To generate a response <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{r}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐫</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{r}}</annotation></semantics></math> given a prompt <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{p}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐩</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{p}}</annotation></semantics></math>, we denoise one block at a time.
Let <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{c}}:=({\mathbf{p}},{\mathbf{r}}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}&lt;b})})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐜</mi><mo>:=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐩</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>𝐫</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#006E37;" mathcolor="#006E37">&lt;</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#006E37;" mathcolor="#006E37">b</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{c}}:=({\mathbf{p}},{\mathbf{r}}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}&lt;b})})</annotation></semantics></math> be the clean context available when generating block <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>b</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b</annotation></semantics></math>, stored in an attention key-value (KV) cache using the AR embeddings.
An offset block-causal mask determines who can see whom (<a href="#S4.F5.sf1" title="In Figure 5 ‣ Score temperature (ST). ‣ 4.2 Trajectory Steering ‣ 4 Language Generation via Continuous Diffusion Sampling ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5(a)</span></a>).
Positions in <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{c}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐜</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{c}}</annotation></semantics></math> use causal attention, so their KV can be cached and reused across diffusion steps, regardless of whether the prompt length is a multiple of <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L^{\prime}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>L</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L^{\prime}</annotation></semantics></math>. Positions in the noisy block <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{z}}_{t}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐳</mi><mi>t</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#006E37;" mathcolor="#006E37">b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{z}}_{t}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})}</annotation></semantics></math> attend bidirectionally within the block and causally to the entire prefix <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{c}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐜</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{c}}</annotation></semantics></math>. After a block is decoded, the AR embeddings of its committed tokens are appended to the causal KV cache for the next block during the next block’s first diffusion step, at no extra NFE.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Sampling block <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>b</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b</annotation></semantics></math> starts from <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{z}}_{1}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})}\sim\mathcal{N}({\mathbf{0}},{\mathbf{I}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐳</mi><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#006E37;" mathcolor="#006E37">b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>𝟎</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>𝐈</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{z}}_{1}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})}\sim\mathcal{N}({\mathbf{0}},{\mathbf{I}})</annotation></semantics></math> and steps from <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s&lt;t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s&lt;t</annotation></semantics></math> along a discretization of <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[1,0]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[1,0]</annotation></semantics></math>.
At each step the denoiser yields a predicted clean embedding <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{\theta}:={\mathbf{e}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{z}}_{t}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})},t;{\mathbf{c}})={\mathbf{x}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{z}}_{t}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})},t;{\mathbf{c}}){\mathbf{E}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐞</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo>:=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐞</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐳</mi><mi>t</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#006E37;" mathcolor="#006E37">b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝐜</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐳</mi><mi>t</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#006E37;" mathcolor="#006E37">b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝐜</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐄</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{\theta}:={\mathbf{e}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{z}}_{t}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})},t;{\mathbf{c}})={\mathbf{x}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{z}}_{t}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})},t;{\mathbf{c}}){\mathbf{E}}</annotation></semantics></math> and the implied noise prediction <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\bm{\epsilon}}_{\theta}:=\frac{1}{\sigma_{t}}({\mathbf{z}}_{t}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})}-\alpha_{t}\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{\theta})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_mathvariant_bold-italic" mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo>:=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐳</mi><mi>t</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#006E37;" mathcolor="#006E37">b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>α</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐞</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>θ</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\bm{\epsilon}}_{\theta}:=\frac{1}{\sigma_{t}}({\mathbf{z}}_{t}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})}-\alpha_{t}\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{\theta})</annotation></semantics></math>.
We introduce two canonical samplers for the reverse process.
The <span id="S4.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">DDPM</span> sampler uses the ancestral kernel of VDM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kingma et al., 2021</a>)</cite>. It draws <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{z}}_{s}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐳</mi><mi>s</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#006E37;" mathcolor="#006E37">b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{z}}_{s}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})}</annotation></semantics></math> from the closed-form Gaussian posterior <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q({\mathbf{z}}_{s}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})}\mid{\mathbf{z}}_{t}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})},{\mathbf{x}}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐳</mi><mi>s</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#006E37;" mathcolor="#006E37">b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐳</mi><mi>t</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#006E37;" mathcolor="#006E37">b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#006E37;" mathcolor="#006E37">b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q({\mathbf{z}}_{s}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})}\mid{\mathbf{z}}_{t}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})},{\mathbf{x}}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})})</annotation></semantics></math> with the clean embedding replaced by <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐞</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math>.
The <span id="S4.SS1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">DDIM</span> sampler <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Song et al., 2021a</a>)</cite> leverages the predictions <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐞</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\bm{\epsilon}}_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_mathvariant_bold-italic" mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\bm{\epsilon}}_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> to deterministically update the state as <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{z}}_{s}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})}=\alpha_{s}\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{\theta}+\sigma_{s}\hat{\bm{\epsilon}}_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐳</mi><mi>s</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#006E37;" mathcolor="#006E37">b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>α</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐞</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>θ</mi></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_mathvariant_bold-italic" mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>θ</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{z}}_{s}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})}=\alpha_{s}\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{\theta}+\sigma_{s}\hat{\bm{\epsilon}}_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math>.
For both samplers, after the final step, tokens are read out as <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\argmax" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>argmax</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\argmax</annotation></semantics></math> of the conditional logit output <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{x}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})},0;{\mathbf{c}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐳</mi><mn>0</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#006E37;" mathcolor="#006E37">b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>𝐜</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{x}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{z}}_{0}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})},0;{\mathbf{c}})</annotation></semantics></math> and appended to <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{c}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐜</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{c}}</annotation></semantics></math>, so <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{NFEs}=\text{steps}+1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext>NFEs</mtext><mo>=</mo><mrow><mtext>steps</mtext><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{NFEs}=\text{steps}+1</annotation></semantics></math>.
See <a href="#alg2" title="In Appendix B Training and Inference Algorithms ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Alg.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> for the complete sampling algorithms and <a href="#A5.SS1" title="E.1 Sampler Updates ‣ Appendix E Implementation Details and Additional Results for Inference ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.1</span></a> for more details.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Trajectory Steering</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To sharpen model predictions, we incorporate two reverse-process steering methods to our blockwise continuous diffusion model with no impact to its training efficiency and minimal impact to its inference efficiency.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Classifier-free guidance (CFG).</h5>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">CFG <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ho and Salimans, 2022</a>)</cite> is the standard tool for class-conditional or text-to-image diffusion models. In CFG, one queries the model twice to obtain a conditional and an unconditional prediction and then linearly extrapolates them.
For our block diffusion model, the clean context <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{c}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐜</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{c}}</annotation></semantics></math> serves as the natural conditioning information, and CFG extrapolates away from the unconditional prediction for the current block <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#006E37;" mathcolor="#006E37">b</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b}</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="S4.EGx6" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S4.Ex4"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.Ex4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle{\mathbf{e}}^{w}_{\theta}({\mathbf{z}}_{t}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})},t;{\mathbf{c}}):={\mathbf{e}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{z}}_{t}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})},t;\varnothing)+w\,\big[{\mathbf{e}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{z}}_{t}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})},t;{\mathbf{c}})-{\mathbf{e}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{z}}_{t}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})},t;\varnothing)\big]," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐞</mi><mi>θ</mi><mi>w</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐳</mi><mi>t</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#006E37;" mathcolor="#006E37">b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝐜</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>:=</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝐞</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐳</mi><mi>t</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#006E37;" mathcolor="#006E37">b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∅</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo lspace="0.170em">⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">[</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝐞</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐳</mi><mi>t</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#006E37;" mathcolor="#006E37">b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝐜</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐞</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐳</mi><mi>t</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#006E37;" mathcolor="#006E37">b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∅</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle{\mathbf{e}}^{w}_{\theta}({\mathbf{z}}_{t}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})},t;{\mathbf{c}}):={\mathbf{e}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{z}}_{t}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})},t;\varnothing)+w\,\big[{\mathbf{e}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{z}}_{t}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})},t;{\mathbf{c}})-{\mathbf{e}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{z}}_{t}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})},t;\varnothing)\big],</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(CFG)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\varnothing" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">∅</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\varnothing</annotation></semantics></math> drops the entire clean context <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{c}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐜</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{c}}</annotation></semantics></math> (so <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{z}}_{t}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐳</mi><mi>t</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#006E37;" mathcolor="#006E37">b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{z}}_{t}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})}</annotation></semantics></math> attends only within its own block) and <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w\geq 1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w\geq 1</annotation></semantics></math> is the guidance strength (<math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w=1</annotation></semantics></math> falls back to the plain conditional prediction).
We bring two technical considerations. First, at batch size <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math> transformer inference is memory-bound, so we pack conditional and unconditional predictions into a single forward pass at almost no wall-clock cost <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2026b</a>)</cite>, using the packed mask of <a href="#S4.F5.sf1" title="In Figure 5 ‣ Score temperature (ST). ‣ 4.2 Trajectory Steering ‣ 4 Language Generation via Continuous Diffusion Sampling ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5(a)</span></a>. We measure this overhead to be less than <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5\%</annotation></semantics></math> per forward pass at block size <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="32" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>32</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">32</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="64" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>64</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">64</annotation></semantics></math> (<a href="#A5.SS9" title="E.9 Wall-Clock Cost of the Packed CFG Forward ‣ Appendix E Implementation Details and Additional Results for Inference ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.9</span></a>).
Second, unlike in image diffusion models and existing dLMs that require train-time context dropout <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Potaptchik et al., 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hu et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">our CFG is a pure inference-time trick</span>: due to sequence packing in pretraining, the first block typically starts in the middle of a document and naturally sees no context.
We discuss existing approaches in <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Related Work ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">App.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Score temperature (ST).</h5>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">ST <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dieleman et al., 2022</a>)</cite> is a heuristic that sharpens the conditional score itself, rescaling the score <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nabla\log p_{t}({\mathbf{z}}_{t}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})}\mid{\mathbf{c}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><mi>log</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐳</mi><mi>t</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#006E37;" mathcolor="#006E37">b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mi>𝐜</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nabla\log p_{t}({\mathbf{z}}_{t}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})}\mid{\mathbf{c}})</annotation></semantics></math> (or equivalently, the noise prediction) by <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{1}{\tau}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>τ</mi></mfrac><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1}{\tau}</annotation></semantics></math> for <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau\in(0,1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau\in(0,1]</annotation></semantics></math>. One can show that it corresponds to the following operation on the mean prediction:</p>
<table id="S4.EGx7" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S4.Ex5"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.Ex5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle{\mathbf{e}}^{\tau}_{\theta}({\mathbf{z}}_{t}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})},t;{\mathbf{c}}):=\tfrac{{\mathbf{z}}_{t}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})}}{\alpha_{t}}+\tfrac{1}{\tau}\big[{\mathbf{e}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{z}}_{t}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})},t;{\mathbf{c}})-\tfrac{{\mathbf{z}}_{t}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})}}{\alpha_{t}}\big]." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐞</mi><mi>θ</mi><mi>τ</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐳</mi><mi>t</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#006E37;" mathcolor="#006E37">b</mi><mo minsize="1.200em">[</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝐞</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐳</mi><mi>t</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#006E37;" mathcolor="#006E37">b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝐜</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><msub><mi>α</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mfrac></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle{\mathbf{e}}^{\tau}_{\theta}({\mathbf{z}}_{t}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})},t;{\mathbf{c}}):=\tfrac{{\mathbf{z}}_{t}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})}}{\alpha_{t}}+\tfrac{1}{\tau}\big[{\mathbf{e}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{z}}_{t}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})},t;{\mathbf{c}})-\tfrac{{\mathbf{z}}_{t}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})}}{\alpha_{t}}\big].</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(ST)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F4" class="ltx_figure ltx_align_floatright" style="width:39%;"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2610.02665v2/tuning_axes.svg" id="S4.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:172/172;" width="172" height="172"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F4.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 4</span>: </span><span id="S4.F4.7" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> <span id="S4.F4.7.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">CFG and ST tuning</span> on <span id="S4.F4.7.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span> -<span id="S4.F4.7.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">unreg</span>-3B for DDPM sampling. Combining both techniques yields larger gains over applying either in isolation, and markedly outperforms sampling without CFG or ST. See <a href="#A5.F15" title="In E.4 Sweeping Classifier-Free Guidance and Score Temperature ‣ Appendix E Implementation Details and Additional Results for Inference ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">15</span></a> for the full tuning grid.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Intuitively, since <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\E[{\mathbf{z}}_{t}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})}|{\mathbf{x}}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})}]=\alpha_{t}{\mathbf{e}}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>𝔼</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐳</mi><mi>t</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#006E37;" mathcolor="#006E37">b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><msup><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#006E37;" mathcolor="#006E37">b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>α</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>𝐞</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#006E37;" mathcolor="#006E37">b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\E[{\mathbf{z}}_{t}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})}|{\mathbf{x}}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})}]=\alpha_{t}{\mathbf{e}}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{1}{\alpha_{t}}{\mathbf{z}}_{t}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msub><mi>α</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐳</mi><mi>t</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#006E37;" mathcolor="#006E37">b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1}{\alpha_{t}}{\mathbf{z}}_{t}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})}</annotation></semantics></math> serves as the naive bad prediction to extrapolate from.
ST does not incur further model queries, and <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau=1</annotation></semantics></math> leaves the sampler unchanged. We also recognize ST as a special case of Temporal Score Rescaling proposed in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xu et al. (2026)</a></cite>.</p>
</div>

<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F5.sf1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">(a)</span> </span><span id="S4.F5.sf1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> Packed attention mask while generating block <math id="S4.F5.sf1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>b</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b</annotation></semantics></math> (<math id="S4.F5.sf1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L^{\prime}=2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>L</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L^{\prime}=2</annotation></semantics></math>). Prefix <math id="S4.F5.sf1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{c}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐜</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{c}}</annotation></semantics></math> is causal (KV-cached). Conditional <math id="S4.F5.sf1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{z}}_{t}^{(b)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐳</mi><mi>t</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{z}}_{t}^{(b)}</annotation></semantics></math> attends to all of <math id="S4.F5.sf1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{c}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐜</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{c}}</annotation></semantics></math> and bidirectionally within the block; unconditional copy attends only to itself.</span></figcaption>

<figure id="S4.F5.sf2" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2610.02665v2/cfg_steering.svg" id="S4.F5.sf2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:429/270;" width="429" height="270"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F5.sf2.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">(b)</span> </span><span id="S4.F5.sf2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> One reverse step <math id="S4.F5.sf2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t\to s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t\to s</annotation></semantics></math>. SC (red) feeds the previous conditional mean (not sharpened by CFG or ST) to the next conditional branch.</span></figcaption>
</figure></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F5.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 5</span>: </span><span id="S4.F5.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Inference<span id="S4.F5.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> for blockwise continuous diffusion: packed CFG attention (a) and one reverse step (b).</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Finally, we remark that due to the commutativity of <a href="#S4.Ex4" title="In Classifier-free guidance (CFG). ‣ 4.2 Trajectory Steering ‣ 4 Language Generation via Continuous Diffusion Sampling ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">CFG</span></a> and <a href="#S4.Ex5" title="Equation ST ‣ Score temperature (ST). ‣ 4.2 Trajectory Steering ‣ 4 Language Generation via Continuous Diffusion Sampling ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">ST</span></a>, we can combine them into a single operation <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{e}}^{w,\tau}_{\theta}({\mathbf{z}}_{t}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})},t;{\mathbf{c}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐞</mi><mi>θ</mi><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐳</mi><mi>t</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#006E37;" mathcolor="#006E37">b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝐜</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{e}}^{w,\tau}_{\theta}({\mathbf{z}}_{t}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})},t;{\mathbf{c}})</annotation></semantics></math>, which is essentially using the score of the composed distribution <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p3.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="(p_{t}(\cdot\mid{\mathbf{c}})^{w}p_{t}(\cdot\mid\varnothing)^{1-w})^{1/\tau}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mi>𝐜</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>w</mi></msup><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∅</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>w</mi></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(p_{t}(\cdot\mid{\mathbf{c}})^{w}p_{t}(\cdot\mid\varnothing)^{1-w})^{1/\tau}</annotation></semantics></math>. We observed that using either knob is weaker than using both of them, see <a href="#S4.F4" title="In Score temperature (ST). ‣ 4.2 Trajectory Steering ‣ 4 Language Generation via Continuous Diffusion Sampling ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Self-conditioning (SC).</h5>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">At inference, SC is applied only to the conditional prediction: when querying the model at time <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math>, the previous step’s conditional prediction <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{e}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{z}}_{t}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})},t;{\mathbf{c}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐞</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐳</mi><mi>t</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#006E37;" mathcolor="#006E37">b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝐜</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{e}}_{\theta}({\mathbf{z}}_{t}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})},t;{\mathbf{c}})</annotation></semantics></math> (before applying CFG and ST) serves as the SC input for the conditional prediction, while the unconditional prediction receives <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{0}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>𝟎</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{0}}</annotation></semantics></math> as the SC input (<a href="#S4.F5.sf2" title="In Figure 5 ‣ Score temperature (ST). ‣ 4.2 Trajectory Steering ‣ 4 Language Generation via Continuous Diffusion Sampling ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5(b)</span></a>).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Sharpening in logit space.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">While in the above, we apply guidance directly in the embedding domain, we can also sharpen in logit space.
In <a href="#A5.SS6" title="E.6 Ablation Study: Steering in Logit Space instead of Embedding Space ‣ Appendix E Implementation Details and Additional Results for Inference ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.6</span></a>, we show that the logit-space CFG and temperature do provide sharpening, but the embedding-space knobs provide stronger performance, hence we keep <a href="#S4.Ex4" title="In Classifier-free guidance (CFG). ‣ 4.2 Trajectory Steering ‣ 4 Language Generation via Continuous Diffusion Sampling ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">CFG</span></a> and <a href="#S4.Ex5" title="Equation ST ‣ Score temperature (ST). ‣ 4.2 Trajectory Steering ‣ 4 Language Generation via Continuous Diffusion Sampling ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">ST</span></a> as the default option.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Embedding Regularization</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We observe that during training, embeddings collapse to approximately 5 effective dimensions (i.e., <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{&gt;}90\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>&gt;</mo><mrow><mn>90</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{&gt;}90\%</annotation></semantics></math> explained variance in the first 5 principal components), a behavior typically not observed in AR language model embeddings but consistent with observations in RePlaid <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2026</a>)</cite>.
This may arise because constant embeddings are a trivial solution for the denoising loss.
We hypothesize that this embedding collapse exacerbates token ambiguity under prediction errors from coarse numerical precision and low-NFE sampling, which motivates regularizing the embeddings toward a uniform distribution on the unit sphere.
For our regularized model <span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span>, we therefore apply a multi-scale extension of <span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sketched Uniform Spherical Regularization</span> (SUSReg, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib65" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nicollier et al. (2026)</a></cite>) to the embedding matrix <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{E}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐄</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{E}}</annotation></semantics></math> during pretraining, penalizing deviations from the uniform distribution on the unit sphere.
We also add a local repulsion loss to push apart very close embedding vectors, and make other minor training changes, see <a href="#A3.SS1" title="C.1 Learning Regularized Embeddings ‣ Appendix C Implementation Details and Additional Results for Pretraining ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.1</span></a> for full details.
We ablate a simpler variant as in the original SUSReg <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib65" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nicollier et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, denoted <span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span> -<span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">preg</span>, which also avoids embedding collapse but is less effective at improving low-NFE quality and distillation (<a href="#A5.T10" title="In Appendix E Implementation Details and Additional Results for Inference ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tabs.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a> and <a href="#A5.T11" title="Table 11 ‣ Appendix E Implementation Details and Additional Results for Inference ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a>); we
report its full benchmark results in <a href="#A3.T6" title="In Full pretrained results for all three variants. ‣ C.1 Learning Regularized Embeddings ‣ Appendix C Implementation Details and Additional Results for Pretraining ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F6" class="ltx_figure ltx_align_floatright" style="width:60%;"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2610.02665v2/mbpp_aime_compact.svg" id="S4.F6.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:286/144;" width="286" height="144"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F6.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 6</span>: </span><span id="S4.F6.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">
<span id="S4.F6.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Left: Pass@<math id="S4.F6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> accuracy on MBPP for <span id="S4.F6.6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span>-3B and <span id="S4.F6.6.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span> -<span id="S4.F6.6.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">distill</span>-3B</span>. All models use pass@1 selected sampler. <span id="S4.F6.6.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Right: Pass@<math id="S4.F6.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> accuracy on AIME 2025 for <span id="S4.F6.6.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span>-3B-Instruct</span>, highlighting best CFG/ST pair chosen from five pre-defined combinations.
</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Results.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As shown in <a href="#S4.T1" title="In 4.4 Mathematical Reasoning and Coding Performance ‣ 4 Language Generation via Continuous Diffusion Sampling ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tabs.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> and <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4.4 Mathematical Reasoning and Coding Performance ‣ 4 Language Generation via Continuous Diffusion Sampling ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, the resulting regularized models <span id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span>-3B/8B achieve the highest average reasoning scores, outperforming NLD <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fu et al., 2026</a>)</cite>. Furthermore, they significantly improve few-step sampling (see <a href="#A5.T10" title="In Appendix E Implementation Details and Additional Results for Inference ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>) and distillation (see <a href="#A6.SS3" title="F.3 Additional Results ‣ Appendix F Implementation Details and Additional Results for Few-step Distillation ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F.3</span></a>) compared to <span id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span> -<span id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">unreg</span>-3B/8B, supporting our hypotheses.
Despite exhibiting substantially different embedding geometries from the unregularized models (<a href="#A3.F10" title="In Sketched Uniform Spherical Regularization (SUSReg). ‣ C.1 Learning Regularized Embeddings ‣ Appendix C Implementation Details and Additional Results for Pretraining ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>), interestingly we find that regularization incurs almost no validation PPL penalty.</p>
</div>
</section>

<div id="S4.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate on two math and four coding benchmarks: GSM8K, Minerva Math, HumanEval, HumanEval+, MBPP, and MBPP+. Results are reported in <a href="#S4.T1" title="In 4.4 Mathematical Reasoning and Coding Performance ‣ 4 Language Generation via Continuous Diffusion Sampling ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>.
For diffusion generation, <span id="S4.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span> models always use SC, and we report performance on DDPM sampling with 256 steps/block with EDM <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho=7" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho=7</annotation></semantics></math> time discretization, and DDIM sampling with 32 steps/block with uniform-<math id="S4.SS4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>γ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma</annotation></semantics></math> time discretization.
See <a href="#A5.SS3" title="E.3 Reasoning and Coding Benchmark Setup ‣ Appendix E Implementation Details and Additional Results for Inference ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.3</span></a> for details on the harness, scoring pipeline, error bar conventions, and the samplers for baselines, and <a href="#A5.SS2" title="E.2 Ablation Study: Time Discretization ‣ Appendix E Implementation Details and Additional Results for Inference ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.2</span></a> for time discretization schemes.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Results.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In AR mode, <span id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span> -<span id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">unreg</span>-3B attains the best six-task average across all methods; in diffusion mode, our DDPM-256 runs are comparable and out-perform NLD-3B on average and sets the best base-model numbers on GSM8K, HumanEval, and HumanEval+; they also outperform LLaDA-8B and Dream-7B by a noticeable margin, despite being <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\sim\!2\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>∼</mo><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim\!2\times</annotation></semantics></math> smaller in parameters. Empirically, we observe <span id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">less</span> left-to-right bias within a block for <span id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span> compared with the confidence-based masked dLM sampling (<a href="#A5.F19" title="In E.10 Reasoning Trajectory Analysis ‣ Appendix E Implementation Details and Additional Results for Inference ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">19</span></a>). To confirm the benefit of AR regularization (<a href="#S3.SS2.SSS2" title="3.2.2 AR Initialization and Regularization ‣ 3.2 Pretraining ‣ 3 Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2.2</span></a>), we also trained <span id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span> -<span id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">unreg</span>-3B with <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\text{BD}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>BD</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\text{BD}}</annotation></semantics></math> alone <a href="#S3.E3" title="In 3.1 Blockwise Probabilistic Model ‣ 3 Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> without <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\text{ar}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>ar</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\text{ar}}</annotation></semantics></math> <a href="#S3.E6" title="In AR Regularization. ‣ 3.2.2 AR Initialization and Regularization ‣ 3.2 Pretraining ‣ 3 Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>; results are uniformly worse across all tasks (<a href="#A5.F16" title="In E.4 Sweeping Classifier-Free Guidance and Score Temperature ‣ Appendix E Implementation Details and Additional Results for Inference ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">16</span></a>). We refer readers to <a href="#S4.T2" title="In 4.4 Mathematical Reasoning and Coding Performance ‣ 4 Language Generation via Continuous Diffusion Sampling ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> for the same evaluation on 8B base models.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Pass@<math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> analysis.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">While pass@<math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math> accuracy in <a href="#S4.T1" title="In 4.4 Mathematical Reasoning and Coding Performance ‣ 4 Language Generation via Continuous Diffusion Sampling ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> captures single-draw quality, test-time search and RL draw multiple rollouts for the same prompt, where diverse rollouts are needed for richer learning signals and increase the chance of discovering a correct solution. Pass@<math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> does not directly measure diversity, but tests whether additional samples expand correct-solution coverage.
We report results in <a href="#S4.F6" title="In 4.3 Embedding Regularization ‣ 4 Language Generation via Continuous Diffusion Sampling ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> on MBPP at the 3B scale, using the same sampler configuration that performs best on pass@<math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math> accuracy with 256 NFEs DDIM sampler.
There, <span id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span>-3B increasingly surpasses as more trials are available, showing that the model has a useful output diversity.
See <a href="#A5.SS8" title="E.8 Pass@𝑘 Evaluation ‣ Appendix E Implementation Details and Additional Results for Inference ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.8</span></a> for the full study.</p>
</div>
</section>
