<section id="S5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.1 </span>ODE Sampler and Time Discretization</h3>

<div id="S5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In previous results, we mainly run 256 DDPM steps per block to establish the strongest performance. In low-NFE regime, it is generally known that deterministic samplers paired with well-tuned time discretization lead to better performance. To investigate the tradeoffs for <span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span>, we choose three representative tasks (GSM8K, HumanEval, and MBPP), and vary the diffusion sampling steps from <math id="S5.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>4</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S5.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="256" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>256</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">256</annotation></semantics></math>. For each sampler-discretization-budget combination, we sweep CFG and ST; we then report, for each combination, the CFG-ST pair that achieves the best average accuracy over the two tasks; see <a href="#A5.SS3" title="E.3 Reasoning and Coding Benchmark Setup ‣ Appendix E Implementation Details and Additional Results for Inference ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.3</span></a> for more details.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Results.</h5>

<div id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As shown in <a href="#A5.F14" title="In E.2 Ablation Study: Time Discretization ‣ Appendix E Implementation Details and Additional Results for Inference ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">14</span></a>, DDIM substantially outperforms DDPM at low NFEs while matching DDPM at high NFEs. The uniform-<math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>γ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma</annotation></semantics></math> discretization (<a href="#A5.SS2" title="E.2 Ablation Study: Time Discretization ‣ Appendix E Implementation Details and Additional Results for Inference ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.2</span></a>) performs the best for a wide range of budgets.
Using the same optimal hyperparameters from the two tasks, we evaluate the 16/32-step performance across all six tasks in <a href="#S4.T1" title="In 4.4 Mathematical Reasoning and Coding Performance ‣ 4 Language Generation via Continuous Diffusion Sampling ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tabs.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> and <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4.4 Mathematical Reasoning and Coding Performance ‣ 4 Language Generation via Continuous Diffusion Sampling ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>; <a href="#A5.T10" title="In Appendix E Implementation Details and Additional Results for Inference ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tabs.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a> and <a href="#A5.T11" title="Table 11 ‣ Appendix E Implementation Details and Additional Results for Inference ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a> show performance at other budgets.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.2 </span>Distribution Matching Distillation for Few-Step Generation</h3>

<div id="S5.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Although DDIM has better performance than DDPM at a reduced generation budget, the pretrained models still lose quality at very low NFEs (especially <math id="S5.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\leq}16" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≤</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\leq}16</annotation></semantics></math> steps, see <a href="#S5.F7" title="In 5 Few-Step Generation ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>). We therefore distill <span id="S5.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span> into a few-step student <span id="S5.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span> -<span id="S5.SS2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">distill</span> using Distribution-Matching Distillation (DMD, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yin et al. (2024b)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib64" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yin et al. (2024a)</a></cite>). Notably, the student uses self-conditioning and a purely stochastic sampler that alternates between clean embedding estimation and fresh Gaussian noise injection, which is different from DDIM sampler. Furthermore, our DMD students are trained to match the target distribution without using CFG, which saves inference FLOPs per NFE compared with the guided teacher, and needs no ST rescaling.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Results.</h5>

<div id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As shown in <a href="#S5.F7" title="In 5 Few-Step Generation ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figs.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>, <a href="#S5.F8" title="Figure 8 ‣ 5 Few-Step Generation ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>, <a href="#A5.T10" title="Table 10 ‣ Appendix E Implementation Details and Additional Results for Inference ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a> and <a href="#A5.T11" title="Table 11 ‣ Appendix E Implementation Details and Additional Results for Inference ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a>, our distillation recipe yields significant acceleration: with only 8 NFEs (<math id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{TPF}=4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext>TPF</mtext><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{TPF}=4</annotation></semantics></math>), <span id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span> -<span id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">distill</span> matches both NLD <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fu et al., 2026</a>)</cite> and our best-performing 256-NFE DDPM sampler on GSM8K and HumanEval at both 3B and 8B scales. For MBPP, which is a full code generation task, syntactic bugs are introduced at low NFE, but <span id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span> -<span id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">distill</span>-3B is still within 3% accuracy of the 256-step sampler at 8 NFEs. Interestingly, despite significant acceleration, we observe that <span id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span> -<span id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">distill</span>-3B does not lose any diversity compared with its 256-step DDPM teacher (see <a href="#A6.SS3" title="F.3 Additional Results ‣ Appendix F Implementation Details and Additional Results for Few-step Distillation ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F.3</span></a>).
As a result, the distilled model exhibits strong pass@<math id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> performance: both 4- and 8-NFE <span id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span> -<span id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">distill</span>-3B catch up with the 256-NFE DDIM <span id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span>-3B teacher at <math id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k=256" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>256</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k=256</annotation></semantics></math> (see <a href="#S4.F6" title="In 4.3 Embedding Regularization ‣ 4 Language Generation via Continuous Diffusion Sampling ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>).
Together, this suggests the distilled model is well suited for accelerated RL-based alignment and post-training.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Self-Speculative Decoding</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span> trains a block-diffusion stream and a causal AR stream on one backbone, so it can act as its own drafter.
In each round, one denoiser call from pure noise drafts a block of <math id="S6.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L^{\prime}=32" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>L</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>32</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L^{\prime}=32</annotation></semantics></math> tokens.
The AR stream then scores the block in one causal pass, keeps the longest prefix that matches its own greedy tokens, and appends one token of its own <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib76" title="" class="ltx_ref">Leviathan et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fu et al., 2026</a>)</cite>.
The output is therefore the greedy AR output.
A round of two forward passes commits <math id="S6.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{AL}+1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>AL</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{AL}+1</annotation></semantics></math> tokens, where the acceptance length (AL) counts the accepted draft tokens that reach the returned answer.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.p2.1" class="ltx_p">At both 3B and 8B scales, we compare NLD to <span id="S6.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span> -<span id="S6.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">distill</span> (<a href="#S5.SS2" title="5.2 Distribution Matching Distillation for Few-Step Generation ‣ 5 Few-Step Generation ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.2</span></a>) to a post-trained model <span id="S6.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span> -<span id="S6.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">distill</span>-<span id="S6.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">spec</span>, which pairs the same distillation objective as <span id="S6.p2.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span> -<span id="S6.p2.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">distill</span> with an acceptance objective (full details in <a href="#A8.SS4" title="H.4 Acceptance Training of the Distilled Model ‣ Appendix H Implementation Details and Additional Results for Self-Speculative Decoding ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">H.4</span></a>).
We serve with SGLang <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib77" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zheng et al., 2024</a>)</cite> in BF16 on one NVIDIA GB200, one request at a time, and evaluate on GSM8K, HumanEval, and MBPP.
AL is pooled over the prompts whose outputs neither loop nor reach the length cap.
<a href="#A8" title="Appendix H Implementation Details and Additional Results for Self-Speculative Decoding ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">H</span></a> details the protocol and gives further results for the undistilled <span id="S6.p2.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span> with trained drafters.</p>

<section id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Results.</h5>

<div id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#S6.F9" title="In 6 Self-Speculative Decoding ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a> shows speedup and AL, and <a href="#S6.T3" title="In 6 Self-Speculative Decoding ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> shows accuracy and the AL gain over NLD.
Without any drafter training, <span id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span> -<span id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">distill</span>-3B accepts 11–21% more draft tokens per round than NLD-3B, and <span id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span> -<span id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">distill</span>-8B accepts 14–23% more than NLD-8B.
We also show in <a href="#A8.SS3" title="H.3 Undistilled Model and Trained Drafters ‣ Appendix H Implementation Details and Additional Results for Self-Speculative Decoding ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">H.3</span></a> that <span id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span> -<span id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">distill</span>-3B also accepts 15–22% more tokens than the <span id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span>-3B, more than what an adapter trained specifically for improving drafting adds to that model. <span id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span> -<span id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">distill</span>-8B gains also more than the adapter on GSM8K and MBPP and as much on HumanEval (<a href="#A8.SS3" title="H.3 Undistilled Model and Trained Drafters ‣ Appendix H Implementation Details and Additional Results for Self-Speculative Decoding ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">H.3</span></a>).
Further acceptance training (joint distillation and drafter fine-tuning) yields <span id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span> -<span id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.11" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">distill</span>-<span id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.12" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">spec</span>, which accepts another 5–9% more tokens per round and decodes up to 3.18<math id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> (3B) and 4.20<math id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> (8B) faster than AR decoding, ahead of NLD on every benchmark and model size.
In all these experiments, the accuracy remains that of the AR mode in each model, since verification returns the greedy AR output. Therefore the speedup comes at no cost relative to AR decoding with the same model.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S7" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">7 </span>Supervised Fine-Tuning</h2>

<div id="S7.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We apply supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to the pretrained <span id="S7.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span> models with the joint AR and block-diffusion losses, restricting supervision to assistant responses. The complete data processing, optimization recipe, and continuous-diffusion-specific controls are given in <a href="#A7" title="Appendix G Implementation Details and Additional Results for Supervised Fine-Tuning ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">App.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">G</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Results.</h5>

<div id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As shown in <a href="#S7.T4" title="In Results. ‣ 7 Supervised Fine-Tuning ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tabs.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> and <a href="#S7.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ Results. ‣ 7 Supervised Fine-Tuning ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, the average performance of <span id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span> -<span id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">instruct</span> models is on par with NLD at both 3B and 8B scale, and surpasses other open-source masked dLMs like Dream and LLaDA at the 8B scale. For both 3B checkpoints, we partially re-sweep CFG and ST after SFT and observe that the same optima selected on the corresponding pre-SFT models remain statistically tied for best after SFT (<a href="#A7.T20" title="In Post-SFT CFG–ST sweep. ‣ G.2 Evaluation Setup, CFG–ST Sweep, and Full Results ‣ Appendix G Implementation Details and Additional Results for Supervised Fine-Tuning ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">20</span></a>); we therefore retain the pre-SFT settings for the full evaluation.</p>
</div>

<section id="S8" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">8 </span>Conclusions</h2>

<div id="S8.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S8.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We introduced <span id="S8.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Nemotron-Labs-Sigma</span>, a family of large-scale blockwise continuous dLMs obtained by efficient continual pretraining from an AR checkpoint, together with a reverse-diffusion sampling recipe that combines DDPM/DDIM samplers with CFG, ST, and SC.
In diffusion mode, <span id="S8.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span> (3B/8B) outperforms same-size masked dLMs and AR baselines trained under an aligned pipeline, both after pretraining and after SFT, with the most consistent gains on coding.
A sphere-normalized embedding regularization further improves low-NFE sampling and makes model distillation markedly more effective.</p>
</div>
<div id="S8.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S8.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Beyond accuracy, the smoothness of continuous trajectories buys efficiency.
Distribution matching is the strongest of the few-step distillation methods we study: using only 8 NFEs (<math id="S8.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{TPF}=4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext>TPF</mtext><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{TPF}=4</annotation></semantics></math>), <span id="S8.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span> -<span id="S8.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">distill</span>-3B almost matches both NLD <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fu et al., 2026</a>)</cite> and our best-performing 256-NFE DDPM teacher, and it does so without collapsing the teacher’s output distribution, preserving diversity and yielding pass@<math id="S8.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> that keeps improving as <math id="S8.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> grows. Because <span id="S8.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span> carries a causal AR stream on the same backbone, the <span id="S8.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">distilled</span> student can also serve as its own one-call drafter: self-speculative decoding returns the greedy AR output at a <math id="S8.p2.m4" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="3.46\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>3.46</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3.46\times</annotation></semantics></math> average speedup over AR decoding at 8B, against <math id="S8.p2.m5" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="3.04\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>3.04</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3.04\times</annotation></semantics></math> for NLD.</p>
</div>
<div id="S8.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S8.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Together, these results establish continuous dLMs as a practical path to efficient language generation.
Looking ahead, the controllable quality–diversity trade-off and the shared diffusion/AR backbone make them particularly attractive for RL-based post-training, which we leave to future work.</p>
</div>
</section>

<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix">Contents</h2>

<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>
<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Related Work</h2>

<div id="A1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">[Back to <a href="#S1" title="1 Introduction ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> or <a href="#S2" title="2 Background ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> in the main paper.]</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">This appendix provides a literature review on continuous diffusion language models, the family to which <span id="A1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span> belongs.</p>
</div>
<section id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Continuous diffusion language models.</h5>

<div id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Continuous dLMs lift discrete tokens into a Euclidean space and run a Gaussian (or Riemannian) diffusion there. A central attraction for doing so is that the machinery developed for image diffusion, such as efficient ODE solvers, guidance, and distillation techniques, transfers with little modification. Existing methods differ mainly in <em id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">where</em> the diffusion process lives:</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<ul id="A1.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="A1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Diffusing <em id="A1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">token embeddings</em>. Diffusion-LM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2022</a>)</cite> pioneered this approach with Gaussian diffusion over learned word embeddings and a rounding step back to tokens; CDCD <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dieleman et al., 2022</a>)</cite> refined the objective with score interpolation and a categorical cross-entropy loss over softmax logits, and self-conditioned embedding diffusion <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Strudel et al., 2022</a>)</cite> added self-conditioning on the previous denoising estimate. Plaid <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gulrajani and Hashimoto, 2023</a>)</cite> tied these ideas together around a likelihood target by pairing low-dimensional sphere-normalized embeddings with a learned noise schedule and categorical reparameterization; RePlaid <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2026</a>)</cite> aligns this recipe with modern DiT architectures and shows it scales competitively with discrete dLMs. Meanwhile, LangFlow <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2026</a>)</cite> follows the same learnable-embedding but uses cross-entropy training loss, while <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib81" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al. (2026)</a></cite> adopts a stochastic-localization formulation. <math id="A1.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{S}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝕊</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{S}</annotation></semantics></math>-FLM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Deschenaux and Gulcehre, 2026</a>)</cite> and Spherical Flows <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib80" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chemseddine et al., 2026</a>)</cite> likewise use learnable token embeddings but further constrain the diffusion trajectory itself to the embedding hypersphere. A parallel strand fixes the embedding to be <em id="A1.I1.i1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">one-hot</em> rather than learned: FLM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lee et al., 2026</a>)</cite> and DFM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Potaptchik et al., 2026</a>)</cite> run flow matching from a Gaussian source to one-hot vocabulary targets in <math id="A1.I1.i1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{R}^{V}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>V</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{R}^{V}</annotation></semantics></math>, and further distill the flow into a few-step flow map for fast generation.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Diffusing an <em id="A1.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">autoencoded latent</em>. Here, a text autoencoder produces a compact continuous latent variable and diffusion is run in that latent space. LD4LG <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lovelace et al., 2023</a>)</cite> runs latent diffusion on a frozen encoder–decoder (BART and T5); COSMOS <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Meshchaninov et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, ELF <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hu et al., 2026</a>)</cite> Cola-DLM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">Guo et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, and AURORA-LM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liang et al., 2026</a>)</cite> scale this axis with different latent designs and training objectives; LDLM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Meshchaninov et al., 2026</a>)</cite> learns the encoder and the diffusion prior jointly rather than sequentially.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Diffusing on the <em id="A1.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">simplex or other statistical manifolds</em>. These methods parameterize a categorical distribution over the vocabulary and diffuse its parameters directly, keeping the noise process on-manifold and avoiding a rounding step. SSD-LM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Han et al., 2023</a>)</cite> runs simplex diffusion in a semi-autoregressive block structure, Dirichlet diffusion <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Avdeyev et al., 2023</a>)</cite> uses a Jacobi diffusion process on the probability simplex, and later variants <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cheng et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Davis et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jo and Hwang, 2025</a>)</cite> extend the geometry to Fisher–Rao and Riemannian flow matching.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A1.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A1.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Reaching discrete data through <em id="A1.I1.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">dequantization or a Gaussian–discrete duality</em>. Argmax flows <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hoogeboom et al., 2021</a>)</cite> lift categorical data into a continuous space via argmax-based variational dequantization, so continuous flows can be trained under a discrete likelihood; analog bits <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, BitLM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhuang et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, and CoBit <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Batzolis et al., 2026</a>)</cite> instead map each token to a bitstring and diffuse from there; Duo <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sahoo et al., 2025</a>)</cite> establishes a duality between continuous Gaussian and uniform-state discrete diffusion, letting the two families share training and sampling machinery.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
<p id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span> sits in the token-embedding class, inheriting the learnable embedding and variational diffusion process of Plaid and RePlaid.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Scaling continuous dLMs to billions of parameters.</h5>

<div id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Recent work pushes continuous dLMs into the billion-parameter regime, but along axes different from ours: for example, Cola-DLM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">Guo et al., 2026</a>)</cite> (<math id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>2B, hierarchical latent-prior modeling), AURORA-LM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liang et al., 2026</a>)</cite> (1B, flow matching over an autoencoded latent), and Categorical Flow Maps <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib75" title="" class="ltx_ref">Davis et al., 2026</a>)</cite> (1.7B, self-distilled for few-step generation). A separate line changes the base representation and scales through an existing LM backbone: BitLM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhuang et al., 2026</a>)</cite> places a bitwise diffusion head atop a causal LM up to 8B, TESS 2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tae et al., 2025</a>)</cite> adapts an autoregressive Mistral-7B into a generalist diffusion model with a simplex cross-entropy loss, and DSL-LLaDA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib82" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al., 2026</a>)</cite> scales continuous denoising via discrete stochastic localization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib81" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2026</a>)</cite> on top of the LLaDA-8B masked-diffusion backbone <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nie et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. In contrast, <span id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span> is, to our knowledge, the first likelihood-trained continuous dLM at 3B/8B, and the first evaluated head-to-head with a matched masked dLM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fu et al., 2026</a>)</cite> on conditional reasoning and code.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">CFG in dLMs.</h5>

<div id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Continuous dLMs realize the guidance condition in two ways. When there is no prompt (e.g., unconditional generation), several works repurpose the self-conditioning signal as the condition: ELF <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hu et al., 2026</a>)</cite> and AURORA-LM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liang et al., 2026</a>)</cite> extrapolate between predictions made with and without the previous-step estimate. For conditional generation, DFM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Potaptchik et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, AURORA-LM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liang et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, Cola-DLM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">Guo et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, and BitLM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhuang et al., 2026</a>)</cite> extrapolate between a prompt-conditioned and an unconditional prediction, as in image diffusion models. A cost for this is that enabling it requires dropping the prompt context during training. FLM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lee et al., 2026</a>)</cite> also leverages autoguidance <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib62" title="" class="ltx_ref">Karras et al., 2024</a>)</cite> for prediction sharpening.
For discrete dLMs, LLaDA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nie et al., 2025</a>)</cite> popularized an “unsupervised” CFG that runs one forward with full prompt and one with the prompt masked, then linearly extrapolates the two logit vectors before renormalizing; this has since been refined by more general discrete guidance mechanisms <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schiff et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nisonoff et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
Our steering (<a href="#S4.SS2" title="4.2 Trajectory Steering ‣ 4 Language Generation via Continuous Diffusion Sampling ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.2</span></a>) differs on three points: (<span id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">i</span>) the guidance condition is the clean prefix itself, and the unconditional branch simply drops that prefix so the noisy block attends only within itself; (<span id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">ii</span>) the extrapolation acts on the predicted clean embedding (equivalently the score), not on logits; (<span id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">iii</span>) it is a pure inference-time operation that requires no train-time dropout because sequence packing leaves the first block without context.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Autoregressive and block video diffusion.</h5>

<div id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our block-causal factorization (i.e., autoregressive across blocks, bidirectional Gaussian denoising within a block over a KV-cacheable clean prefix) closely mirrors recent video generation models that couple causal structure across frames with denoising within them <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yin et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib61" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. The bidirectional video-diffusion lineage <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ho et al., 2022</a>)</cite> was the original target of this conversion, and the autoregressive arm of Cosmos <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Agarwal et al., 2025</a>)</cite> likewise structures video generation causally across frames. Diffusion Forcing <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2024</a>)</cite> trains a causal model with independent per-frame noise levels, unifying next-token prediction with full-sequence diffusion and enabling stable rollouts past the training horizon. CausVid <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yin et al., 2025</a>)</cite> and Self Forcing <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib61" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huang et al., 2025</a>)</cite> convert bidirectional video diffusion into causal, KV-cached autoregressive generators for fast streaming synthesis while curbing error accumulation along the rollout. These works share our central design tension (i.e., coupling causal, autoregressive structure with within-block diffusion) and several of their techniques (per-block noise schedules, rolling KV caches, distribution-matching distillation) transfer naturally to the language setting.</p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>
</section>

alttext="{\mathbf{x}}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}&lt;b})}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#006E37;" mathcolor="#006E37">&lt;</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#006E37;" mathcolor="#006E37">b</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{x}}^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}&lt;b})}</annotation></semantics></math> and bidirectionally within itself, so a per-block time <math id="A2.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>t</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#006E37;" mathcolor="#006E37">b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})}</annotation></semantics></math> and a per-block Horvitz–Thompson coin <math id="A2.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>R</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi style="--ltx-fg-color:#006E37;" mathcolor="#006E37">b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R^{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.2148}b})}</annotation></semantics></math> cost no extra compute. At inference, the conditional and unconditional branches are likewise packed into one forward as in <a href="#S4.F5.sf1" title="In Figure 5 ‣ Score temperature (ST). ‣ 4.2 Trajectory Steering ‣ 4 Language Generation via Continuous Diffusion Sampling ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5(a)</span></a>, so the guidance computation costs slightly more wall-clock time per step (<a href="#A5.T19" title="In E.9 Wall-Clock Cost of the Packed CFG Forward ‣ Appendix E Implementation Details and Additional Results for Inference ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">19</span></a>) at batch size one.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">The losses are sequence sums, so per-token embedding penalties carry a factor <math id="A2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>L</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L</annotation></semantics></math>. For MS-SUSReg, <math id="A2.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda_{\text{susreg}}=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>λ</mi><mtext>susreg</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda_{\text{susreg}}=1</annotation></semantics></math> because <math id="A2.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{\mathrm{MS}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>MS</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{\mathrm{MS}}</annotation></semantics></math> already includes the scale weights. SC-selected sequences stop NELBO gradients to the diffusion embedding and schedule while retaining regularizer gradients. MS-SUSReg balances the <math id="A2.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="25\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>25</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">25\%</annotation></semantics></math> SC fraction across each global batch.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">We further clarify on the learning of the noise schedule, since its two parts are optimized for two different objectives.
The endpoints <math id="A2.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma_{0},\gamma_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>γ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>γ</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma_{0},\gamma_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> enter <math id="A2.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\text{diff}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>diff</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\text{diff}}</annotation></semantics></math> through <math id="A2.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\operatorname{SNR}^{\prime}(t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>SNR</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\operatorname{SNR}^{\prime}(t)</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A2.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\alpha_{t},\sigma_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>α</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\alpha_{t},\sigma_{t})</annotation></semantics></math>, so they receive an ordinary NELBO gradient and are trained to tighten the bound while the interior shape <math id="A2.p5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{\gamma}_{\psi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>γ</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>ψ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{\gamma}_{\psi}</annotation></semantics></math> does not. As noted in <a href="#S2" title="2 Background ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, the diffusion term is invariant to it in expectation, so <math id="A2.p5.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nabla_{\psi}\mathcal{L}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mo>∇</mo><mi>ψ</mi></msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nabla_{\psi}\mathcal{L}</annotation></semantics></math> is zero on average and carries only noise. Following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kingma et al. (2021)</a></cite>, <math id="A2.p5.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\psi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ψ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\psi</annotation></semantics></math> is instead trained to minimize the Monte-Carlo variance of the diffusion estimator, which for a mean-invariant estimator reduces to minimizing its second moment <math id="A2.p5.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\text{var}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>var</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\text{var}}</annotation></semantics></math> in <a href="#alg1" title="In Appendix B Training and Inference Algorithms ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Alg.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>. In code, each block’s schedule gradient is scaled by twice its detached mean diffusion loss; reconstruction blocks and SC-selected sequences do not update the shape.
Variant-specific optimizer and learning-rate settings are given in <a href="#A3.SS1" title="C.1 Learning Regularized Embeddings ‣ Appendix C Implementation Details and Additional Results for Pretraining ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.1</span></a>.</p>
</div>

<div id="A2.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.p6.1" class="ltx_p">The outer loop of <a href="#alg2" title="In Appendix B Training and Inference Algorithms ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Alg.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> runs <math id="A2.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B:=\lceil T_{\text{gen}}/S\rceil" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>:=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">⌈</mo><mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mtext>gen</mtext></msub><mo>/</mo><mi>S</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">⌉</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B:=\lceil T_{\text{gen}}/S\rceil</annotation></semantics></math> times, and each window costs <math id="A2.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N+1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N+1</annotation></semantics></math> denoiser forward passes (<math id="A2.p6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> diffusion steps plus one decoding readout), for a total of <math id="A2.p6.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B(N+1)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B(N+1)</annotation></semantics></math> forward passes. The effective NFE per committed token is thus <math id="A2.p6.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\approx(N+1)/S" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≈</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>/</mo><mi>S</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\approx(N+1)/S</annotation></semantics></math>,
see <a href="#A5.SS7" title="E.7 Ablation Study: Commit-Stride Sampling ‣ Appendix E Implementation Details and Additional Results for Inference ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.7</span></a> for a full compute-vs-quality sweep.
Setting <math id="A2.p6.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w=1</annotation></semantics></math> disables CFG, <math id="A2.p6.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau=1</annotation></semantics></math> disables ST, and never updating <math id="A2.p6.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{e}}_{\text{sc}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐞</mi><mtext>sc</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{e}}_{\text{sc}}</annotation></semantics></math> (i.e., leaving it as <math id="A2.p6.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{0}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>𝟎</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{0}}</annotation></semantics></math>) disables SC; each of these recovers a strictly weaker sampler, as shown in <a href="#A5.F15" title="In E.4 Sweeping Classifier-Free Guidance and Score Temperature ‣ Appendix E Implementation Details and Additional Results for Inference ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">15</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>
<section id="A3" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix C </span>Implementation Details and Additional Results for Pretraining</h2>

<div id="A3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">[Back to <a href="#S3.SS2" title="3.2 Pretraining ‣ 3 Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a> in the main paper.]</p>
</div>
<section id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Architecture.</h5>

<div id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Following NLD <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fu et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, we adopt the transformer architecture of Ministral <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2026a</a>)</cite>:</p>
<ul id="A3.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="A3.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A3.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">3B: 26 layers, width 3072, FFN
9216, 32 query and 8 key/value heads (head dimension 128), SwiGLU, RMSNorm, YaRN-scaled rotary
embeddings (<math id="A3.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta=10^{6}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mn>6</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta=10^{6}</annotation></semantics></math>), and untied embeddings. This adds up to 3.0B non-embedding and 3.8B total
parameters.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A3.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A3.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">8B: 34 layers, width 4096, FFN 14336, same 32 query and 8 key/value heads (head
dimension 128) and same SwiGLU, RMSNorm, YaRN rotary embeddings and untied embeddings. This adds up to 7.4B
non-embedding and 8.5B total parameters.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Optimization.</h5>

<div id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For <span id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span> -<span id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">unreg</span>/<span id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span> -<span id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">preg</span>, <math id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{\gamma}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>γ</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{\gamma}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{E}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐄</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{E}}</annotation></semantics></math> use AdamW with <math id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta_{1}=0.9" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>β</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.9</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta_{1}=0.9</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta_{2}=0.95" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>β</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.95</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta_{2}=0.95</annotation></semantics></math>, no weight decay (rows of <math id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{E}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐄</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{E}}</annotation></semantics></math> unit-norm), and peak learning rate <math id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\eta_{\text{peak}}=1\times 10^{-2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>η</mi><mtext>peak</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\eta_{\text{peak}}=1\times 10^{-2}</annotation></semantics></math>; <math id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma_{0},\gamma_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>γ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>γ</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma_{0},\gamma_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> use the same setting but with weight decay <math id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.1</annotation></semantics></math> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2026</a>)</cite>. For other parameters, we follow NLD and use AdamW with <math id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta_{1}=0.9" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>β</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.9</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta_{1}=0.9</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta_{2}=0.95" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>β</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.95</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta_{2}=0.95</annotation></semantics></math>, weight decay <math id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.1</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\eta_{\text{peak}}=1\times 10^{-5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>η</mi><mtext>peak</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\eta_{\text{peak}}=1\times 10^{-5}</annotation></semantics></math>. For all parameters, we use gradient clipping value <math id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1.0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1.0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.0</annotation></semantics></math>. The learning rate schedule is Warmup-Stable-Decay over 150k steps: <math id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1\%</annotation></semantics></math> linear warmup to <math id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\eta_{\text{peak}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>η</mi><mtext>peak</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\eta_{\text{peak}}</annotation></semantics></math>, constant
through step 120k, then exponential decay to <math id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>10</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10\%</annotation></semantics></math> of <math id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\eta_{\text{peak}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>η</mi><mtext>peak</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\eta_{\text{peak}}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Self-conditioning (SC).</h5>

<div id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">SC injects the model’s own detached clean-embedding prediction
into the projected noised input stream with a bias-free, zero-initialized linear layer mapping <math id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{R}^{d_{e}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>e</mi></msub></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{R}^{d_{e}}</annotation></semantics></math> to the hidden width <math id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{R}^{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{R}^{d}</annotation></semantics></math>: a first pass with <math id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{e}}_{\text{sc}}={\mathbf{0}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐞</mi><mtext>sc</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>𝟎</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{e}}_{\text{sc}}={\mathbf{0}}</annotation></semantics></math>, then a second pass with <math id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sqrt{d_{e}}\,\operatorname{sg}({\mathbf{e}}_{\text{sc}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msqrt><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>e</mi></msub></msqrt><mo lspace="0.337em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi>sg</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐞</mi><mtext>sc</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sqrt{d_{e}}\,\operatorname{sg}({\mathbf{e}}_{\text{sc}})</annotation></semantics></math> through that linear layer.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Time conditioning.</h5>

<div id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For diffusion stream, a single <math id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>γ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma</annotation></semantics></math> is sampled per block and shared across its tokens. We encode <math id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>γ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma</annotation></semantics></math> using fixed sinusoidal features with frequencies <math id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\exp(\mathrm{linspace}(-5,5,32))" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>exp</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>linspace</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>32</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\exp(\mathrm{linspace}(-5,5,32))</annotation></semantics></math>, concatenating <math id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[\sin,\cos]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>sin</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>cos</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[\sin,\cos]</annotation></semantics></math> into 64 dimensions. A bias-free, zero-initialized linear layer projects this encoding to the hidden width, where it is added to the projected noised input.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px5" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Numerical precision.</h5>

<div id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Transformer weights and matrix multiplications, including the linear logit heads, use <span id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">BF16</span>; gradient accumulation and communication use <span id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">FP32</span>. The diffusion embedding, noise schedule, gamma endpoints, and input/time/SC projections are stored in <span id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">FP32</span> for MS-SUSReg and <span id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">BF16</span> for <span id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span> -<span id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">unreg</span>/<span id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span> -<span id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">preg</span>. Embedding normalization, corruption, input/time/SC projections, and logit postprocessing compute in <span id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">FP32</span>; projected inputs are cast to <span id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.1.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">BF16</span> for the transformer. Schedule arithmetic and NELBO accumulation use <span id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.1.11" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">FP64</span>, following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gulrajani and Hashimoto (2023)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al. (2026)</a></cite>. Adam moments and master copies of <span id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.1.12" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">BF16</span> weights are <span id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.1.13" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">FP32</span>. Optimizer state is sharded across data-parallel ranks, except for MS-SUSReg’s replicated schedule and endpoint states.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px6" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">AR regularization.</h5>

<div id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For training <span id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span> -<span id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">unreg</span>-3B, we searched over <math id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{\text{diff}}\in\{0.3,1.0\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mtext>diff</mtext></msub><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>0.3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1.0</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{\text{diff}}\in\{0.3,1.0\}</annotation></semantics></math>. Interestingly, when <math id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{\text{diff}}=1.0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mtext>diff</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1.0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{\text{diff}}=1.0</annotation></semantics></math>, adding the AR regularization even improved diffusion PPL (<a href="#S3.F3.sf3" title="In Figure 3 ‣ 3.2 Pretraining ‣ 3 Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3(c)</span></a>). However, we found that switching to <math id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{\text{diff}}=0.3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mtext>diff</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{\text{diff}}=0.3</annotation></semantics></math> at 200B tokens (equivalently, <math id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="100\text{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>100</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>k</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">100\text{k}</annotation></semantics></math> steps) offers the best convergence for both losses (<a href="#S3.F3.sf3" title="In Figure 3 ‣ 3.2 Pretraining ‣ 3 Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3(c)</span></a>). We thus adopted this schedule (<math id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{\text{diff}}=1.0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mtext>diff</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1.0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{\text{diff}}=1.0</annotation></semantics></math> for the first <math id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="100\text{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>100</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>k</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">100\text{k}</annotation></semantics></math> steps and <math id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{\text{diff}}=0.3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mtext>diff</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{\text{diff}}=0.3</annotation></semantics></math> for the last <math id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="50\text{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>50</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>k</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">50\text{k}</annotation></semantics></math> steps) for all of our <span id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span> -<span id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">unreg</span>-3B/8B and <span id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span> -<span id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">preg</span>-3B/8B models (see <a href="#A3.SS1" title="C.1 Learning Regularized Embeddings ‣ Appendix C Implementation Details and Additional Results for Pretraining ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.1</span></a>). For <span id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span>-3B/8B, we keep <math id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{\text{diff}}=1.0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mtext>diff</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1.0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{\text{diff}}=1.0</annotation></semantics></math> all the way through <math id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="150\text{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>150</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>k</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">150\text{k}</annotation></semantics></math> steps for simplicity of the training objective.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">C.1 </span>Learning Regularized Embeddings</h3>

<div id="A3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">[Back to <a href="#S4.SS3" title="4.3 Embedding Regularization ‣ 4 Language Generation via Continuous Diffusion Sampling ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.3</span></a> in the main paper.]</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The central goal for our embedding-regularized model variants is to improve the low-NFE performance and distillability by improving the structure of the embeddings.
To this end, we develop the toolbox described in the following: A multiscale variant of Sketched Uniform Spherical Regularization (SUSReg) and a local repulsion loss to combat global and local embedding collapse; a modified Riemannian Adam optimizer step for the embedding table that respects the per-row hyperspherical geometry; a simpler noise schedule parameterization based on Bernstein polynomials that can be trivially initialized to a linear (log-SNR) shape, together with a custom projected optimizer step; and a cosine learning rate schedule for the embeddings to aid their stable learning.</p>
</div>
<section id="A3.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Sketched Uniform Spherical Regularization (SUSReg).</h5>

<div id="A3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To avoid the <math id="A3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V=131072" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>V</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>131072</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V=131072</annotation></semantics></math> embedding vectors in <math id="A3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{e}=16" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{e}=16</annotation></semantics></math> dimensional unit sphere being too tightly clustered for accurate decoding (as observed in their low-rank structure in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al. (2026)</a></cite>), we propose to add an optional regularization term based on SUSReg <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib65" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nicollier et al., 2026</a>)</cite> to the embeddings, which regularizes their distribution <math id="A3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{\mathbf{E}}:=\frac{1}{V}\sum_{v=1}^{V}\delta_{{\mathbf{e}}_{v}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>𝐄</mi></msub><mo>:=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>V</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>V</mi></msubsup><msub><mi>δ</mi><msub><mi>𝐞</mi><mi>v</mi></msub></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{\mathbf{E}}:=\frac{1}{V}\sum_{v=1}^{V}\delta_{{\mathbf{e}}_{v}}</annotation></semantics></math> toward <math id="A3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\operatorname{Unif}(\mathbb{S}^{d_{e}-1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Unif</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>𝕊</mi><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\operatorname{Unif}(\mathbb{S}^{d_{e}-1})</annotation></semantics></math>, the uniform distribution on the unit sphere in <math id="A3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{R}^{d_{e}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>e</mi></msub></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{R}^{d_{e}}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
