<section id="A5.SS7.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Results.</h5>

<div id="A5.SS7.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.SS7.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We present the results for commit-stride sampling for <span id="A5.SS7.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span> -<span id="A5.SS7.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">unreg</span>-3B/8B in <a href="#A5.T17" title="In Nominal vs. true NFE. ‣ E.7 Ablation Study: Commit-Stride Sampling ‣ Appendix E Implementation Details and Additional Results for Inference ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tabs.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">17</span></a> and <a href="#A5.T18" title="Table 18 ‣ Nominal vs. true NFE. ‣ E.7 Ablation Study: Commit-Stride Sampling ‣ Appendix E Implementation Details and Additional Results for Inference ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">18</span></a>, respectively. The tables sweep all three strides <math id="A5.SS7.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S\in\{8,16,32\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>16</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>32</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S\in\{8,16,32\}</annotation></semantics></math> within each nominal-NFE bucket <math id="A5.SS7.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{256,128,64,32\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>256,128</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>64</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>32</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{256,128,64,32\}</annotation></semantics></math>. At the top NFE (nominal <math id="A5.SS7.SSS0.Px3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="256" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>256</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">256</annotation></semantics></math>), the DDIM <math id="A5.SS7.SSS0.Px3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="64" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>64</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">64</annotation></semantics></math> steps / stride <math id="A5.SS7.SSS0.Px3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>8</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">8</annotation></semantics></math> row is the best on both models: it beats the tuned DDPM-256 baseline of <a href="#S4.T1" title="In 4.4 Mathematical Reasoning and Coding Performance ‣ 4 Language Generation via Continuous Diffusion Sampling ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tabs.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> and <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4.4 Mathematical Reasoning and Coding Performance ‣ 4 Language Generation via Continuous Diffusion Sampling ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> by <math id="A5.SS7.SSS0.Px3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+2.66" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>2.66</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+2.66</annotation></semantics></math> average points on 3B and <math id="A5.SS7.SSS0.Px3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+0.76" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>0.76</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+0.76</annotation></semantics></math> on 8B, with the largest per-task gains on the coding benchmarks such as MBPP. The same ordering holds down to around nominal <math id="A5.SS7.SSS0.Px3.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="64" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>64</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">64</annotation></semantics></math>: committing fewer tokens per window (i.e., smaller stride <math id="A5.SS7.SSS0.Px3.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>S</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S</annotation></semantics></math>) improves the average monotonically. At nominal <math id="A5.SS7.SSS0.Px3.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="128" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>128</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">128</annotation></semantics></math> NFE, DDIM <math id="A5.SS7.SSS0.Px3.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="32" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>32</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">32</annotation></semantics></math> steps / stride <math id="A5.SS7.SSS0.Px3.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>8</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">8</annotation></semantics></math> reaches within a point of the top budget on both sizes, and still above the full-stride DDPM-256 baselines. The benefit of a smaller stride disappears once it forces the per-window step count below roughly <math id="A5.SS7.SSS0.Px3.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="16" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>16</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">16</annotation></semantics></math>: at nominal <math id="A5.SS7.SSS0.Px3.p1.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="32" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>32</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">32</annotation></semantics></math>, stride <math id="A5.SS7.SSS0.Px3.p1.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>8</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">8</annotation></semantics></math> leaves only <math id="A5.SS7.SSS0.Px3.p1.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>8</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">8</annotation></semantics></math> steps per window, and its coarse time grid collapses quality due to larger discretization error, falling below the stride-<math id="A5.SS7.SSS0.Px3.p1.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="16" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>16</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">16</annotation></semantics></math> and stride-<math id="A5.SS7.SSS0.Px3.p1.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="32" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>32</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">32</annotation></semantics></math> rows at the same budget.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A5.SS8" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">E.8 </span>Pass@<math id="A5.SS8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> Evaluation
</h3>

<div id="A5.SS8.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.SS8.p1.1" class="ltx_p">[Back to <a href="#S4.T2" title="In 4.4 Mathematical Reasoning and Coding Performance ‣ 4 Language Generation via Continuous Diffusion Sampling ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> in the main paper.]</p>
</div>
<div id="A5.SS8.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.SS8.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We study inference-time scaling in two distinct evaluation regimes.
First, we compare the pretrained 3B models on MBPP;
second, we compare the instruct 3B models on AIME 2025.</p>
</div>
<section id="A5.SS8.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">MBPP for base models.</h5>

<figure id="A5.F17" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2610.02665v2/mbpp_per_k_vs_pass1_measured.svg" id="A5.F17.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:429/178;" width="429" height="178"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A5.F17.9" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 17</span>: </span><span id="A5.F17.10" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">
<span id="A5.F17.10.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Pass@<math id="A5.F17.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> on MBPP of <span id="A5.F17.10.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span>-3B, <span id="A5.F17.10.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span> -<span id="A5.F17.10.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">distill</span>-3B and NLD-3B.</span>
<em id="A5.F17.10.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Left:</em> At each <math id="A5.F17.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>, each family uses the best configuration in its tested sampler grid;
<em id="A5.F17.10.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Right:</em> Fixed sampler configuration picked by highest pass@<math id="A5.F17.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math> accuracy: NLD-3B <math id="A5.F17.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\vartheta=0.9,T=0.3)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>ϑ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.9</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.3</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\vartheta=0.9,T=0.3)</annotation></semantics></math>, <span id="A5.F17.10.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span>-3B <math id="A5.F17.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(DDPM,w=2,\tau=0.1)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>D</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>P</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(DDPM,w=2,\tau=0.1)</annotation></semantics></math>, <span id="A5.F17.10.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span> -<span id="A5.F17.10.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">distill</span>-3B have a fixed sampler (no CFG/ST).
</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A5.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We compare <span id="A5.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span>-3B, <span id="A5.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span> -<span id="A5.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">distill</span>-3B and NLD-3B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fu et al., 2026</a>)</cite> on MBPP, drawing 256 generations per problem for every configuration. Both models use block size 32. <span id="A5.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span>-3B uses DDPM with 256 steps/block and the EDM <math id="A5.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho=7" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho=7</annotation></semantics></math> schedule, sweeping CFG <math id="A5.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w\in\{1,2,3\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w\in\{1,2,3\}</annotation></semantics></math> and ST <math id="A5.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau\in\{0.1,0.4,0.7,1.0\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>0.1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.7</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1.0</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau\in\{0.1,0.4,0.7,1.0\}</annotation></semantics></math>; NLD-3B uses 32 transfer steps per block, sweeping confidence threshold <math id="A5.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\vartheta\in\{0.8,0.9\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϑ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>0.8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.9</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\vartheta\in\{0.8,0.9\}</annotation></semantics></math> and temperature <math id="A5.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T\in\{0.3,0.6,1.0\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>0.3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.6</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1.0</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T\in\{0.3,0.6,1.0\}</annotation></semantics></math>; <span id="A5.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span> -<span id="A5.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">distill</span>-3B use 4 and 8 NFEs and dedicated sampler without any post-hoc guidance. Candidate draws use different random seeds while preserving identical prompts and few-shot examples across configurations, as in <a href="#A5.SS3" title="E.3 Reasoning and Coding Benchmark Setup ‣ Appendix E Implementation Details and Additional Results for Inference ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.3</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A5.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The left panel of <a href="#A5.F17" title="In MBPP for base models. ‣ E.8 Pass@𝑘 Evaluation ‣ Appendix E Implementation Details and Additional Results for Inference ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">17</span></a> shows the best performance available in each tested sampler grid at every generation budget. As <math id="A5.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> grows, the <span id="A5.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span>-3B setting carrying this curve moves from <math id="A5.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau=0.1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau=0.1</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="A5.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.4</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.4</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A5.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.7" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.7</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.7</annotation></semantics></math>, and finally <math id="A5.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1.0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1.0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.0</annotation></semantics></math>, shifting from single-sample quality toward broader coverage.
the right panel provides the complementary fixed-configuration result tuned on pass@1 (i.e. that in <a href="#S4.T1" title="In 4.4 Mathematical Reasoning and Coding Performance ‣ 4 Language Generation via Continuous Diffusion Sampling ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>).
<span id="A5.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span>-3B consistently beats NLD=3B by a small, almost constant margin.
However, most interesting is the behavior of <span id="A5.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span> -<span id="A5.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">distill</span>-3B which with only 8-NFEs matches the <span id="A5.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span>-3B teacher from <math id="A5.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k=32" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>32</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k=32</annotation></semantics></math> onward, and the 4-NFE version closes the gap as <math id="A5.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> increases, finally matching <span id="A5.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span>-3B at <math id="A5.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k=256" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>256</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k=256</annotation></semantics></math>.
This demonstrates that our distilled models exercise <span id="A5.SS8.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">useful</span> diversity.</p>
</div>

<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">AIME 2025 for instruct models.</h5>

<div id="A5.SS8.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.SS8.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We repeat the comparison on the <em id="A5.SS8.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">instruct</em> models, under the same protocol as the benchmark table in <a href="#S7.T4" title="In Results. ‣ 7 Supervised Fine-Tuning ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> (harness described in <a href="#A7.SS2" title="G.2 Evaluation Setup, CFG–ST Sweep, and Full Results ‣ Appendix G Implementation Details and Additional Results for Supervised Fine-Tuning ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">G.2</span></a>), on AIME 2025.
<span id="A5.SS8.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span>-3B–<span id="A5.SS8.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">instruct</span> uses DDIM with 32 steps and the uniform-<math id="A5.SS8.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>γ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma</annotation></semantics></math> schedule, sweeping the five settings <math id="A5.SS8.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(w,\tau)\in\{(3,0.3),\,(4,0.3),\,(4,0.7),\,(5,0.7),\,(3,1.0)\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>w</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.337em">,</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.337em">,</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.7</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.337em">,</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.7</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.337em">,</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1.0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(w,\tau)\in\{(3,0.3),\,(4,0.3),\,(4,0.7),\,(5,0.7),\,(3,1.0)\}</annotation></semantics></math>; NLD-3B-Instruct uses confidence-threshold masked decoding with <math id="A5.SS8.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\vartheta=0.9" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϑ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.9</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\vartheta=0.9</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A5.SS8.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T\in\{0.2,0.6,1.0\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>0.2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.6</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1.0</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T\in\{0.2,0.6,1.0\}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>

<p id="A5.SS8.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The response budgets are 4096 tokens for <span id="A5.SS8.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span>-3B–<span id="A5.SS8.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">instruct</span> and 16384 for NLD-3B-Instruct, but the shorter <span id="A5.SS8.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span> cap is not binding since the reasonable generations (i.e., the samples that are not degenerate, such as repeating the same pattern without emitting EOS token) are all within this length range for both models.
The results are in <a href="#A5.F18" title="In MBPP for base models. ‣ E.8 Pass@𝑘 Evaluation ‣ Appendix E Implementation Details and Additional Results for Inference ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">18</span></a>.</p>

<div id="A5.SS9.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.SS9.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We measure the wall-clock cost of the packed CFG forward with attention mask (<a href="#S4.F5.sf1" title="In Figure 5 ‣ Score temperature (ST). ‣ 4.2 Trajectory Steering ‣ 4 Language Generation via Continuous Diffusion Sampling ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5(a)</span></a>) at batch size <math id="A5.SS9.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math> compared with the unguided forward. We decode the same set of <math id="A5.SS9.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="16" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>16</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">16</annotation></semantics></math> GSM8K questions (<math id="A5.SS9.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>8</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">8</annotation></semantics></math>-shot, prompt length <math id="A5.SS9.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="729\sim 814" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>729</mn><mo>∼</mo><mn>814</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">729\sim 814</annotation></semantics></math>) with the DDIM sampler at <math id="A5.SS9.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="32" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>32</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">32</annotation></semantics></math> steps per block, on the first block only.
Each question therefore requires <math id="A5.SS9.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="32+1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>32</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">32+1</annotation></semantics></math> forward passes (<a href="#alg2" title="In Appendix B Training and Inference Algorithms ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Alg.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>).
The very first denoiser query of each process involves a one-time CUDA initialization which takes a longer time, so is excluded to avoid biasing the measurement. All runs are performed on one NVIDIA H100 GPU, using <span id="A5.SS9.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span> -<span id="A5.SS9.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">unreg</span>-3B with precision <span id="A5.SS9.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">BF16</span>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A5.SS9.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.SS9.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Results in <a href="#A5.T19" title="In E.9 Wall-Clock Cost of the Packed CFG Forward ‣ Appendix E Implementation Details and Additional Results for Inference ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">19</span></a> show that at <math id="A5.SS9.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L^{\prime}=32" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>L</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>32</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L^{\prime}=32</annotation></semantics></math> the packed transformer forward costs <math id="A5.SS9.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+1.8\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mn>1.8</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+1.8\%</annotation></semantics></math> over the unguided one, and at <math id="A5.SS9.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L^{\prime}=64" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>L</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>64</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L^{\prime}=64</annotation></semantics></math> it is free to within measurement noise. The per-NFE overhead is dominated by computing the second set of logits, doing softmax, and multiplying by the embedding matrix rather than by attention.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A5.SS10" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">E.10 </span>Reasoning Trajectory Analysis</h3>

<div id="A5.SS10.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.SS10.p1.1" class="ltx_p">[Back to <a href="#S4.SS4" title="4.4 Mathematical Reasoning and Coding Performance ‣ 4 Language Generation via Continuous Diffusion Sampling ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.4</span></a> in the main paper.]</p>
</div>
<div id="A5.SS10.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.SS10.p2.1" class="ltx_p">As noted in <a href="#S4.T2" title="In 4.4 Mathematical Reasoning and Coding Performance ‣ 4 Language Generation via Continuous Diffusion Sampling ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, we empirically observe less left-to-right bias within a block for <span id="A5.SS10.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span> compared with the confidence-based masked dLM sampling. We demonstrate this in <a href="#A5.F19" title="In E.10 Reasoning Trajectory Analysis ‣ Appendix E Implementation Details and Additional Results for Inference ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">19</span></a>, where we show a commit order analysis between continuous and discrete dLMs.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A5.F19" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2610.02665v2/commitment_order_all_tasks_llaconda-0.9_mdlm-0.9_arxiv.svg" id="A5.F19.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_portrait" style="aspect-ratio:333/499;" width="333" height="499"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A5.F19.7" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 19</span>: </span><span id="A5.F19.8" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> <span id="A5.F19.8.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Token commitment order vs token position for <span id="A5.F19.8.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span> -<span id="A5.F19.8.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">unreg</span>-3B</span>
<span id="A5.F19.8.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span> uses 256-step DDPM (<math id="A5.F19.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w=2,\tau=0.1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w=2,\tau=0.1</annotation></semantics></math>) as in <a href="#S4.T1" title="In 4.4 Mathematical Reasoning and Coding Performance ‣ 4 Language Generation via Continuous Diffusion Sampling ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>. Generation order averaged across multiple documents and blocks. For <span id="A5.F19.8.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span> -<span id="A5.F19.8.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">unreg</span>-3B, the commitment step <math id="A5.F19.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> of position <math id="A5.F19.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math> is defined as the smallest <math id="A5.F19.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> such that for every step <math id="A5.F19.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t^{\prime}\geq t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>t</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>≥</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t^{\prime}\geq t</annotation></semantics></math> up to the final readout, (i) the argmax of <math id="A5.F19.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> equals the finally decoded token, and (ii) that argmax is assigned probability at least <math id="A5.F19.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.9" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.9</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.9</annotation></semantics></math>. The commitment order of position <math id="A5.F19.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math> is the rank of <math id="A5.F19.m19" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> among <math id="A5.F19.m20" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{t_{1},\dots,t_{32}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>t</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mn>32</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{t_{1},\dots,t_{32}}</annotation></semantics></math> within its block, in ascending order. Positions sharing a commitment step share the lowest rank of the tie.</span></figcaption>

<section id="A6" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix F </span>Implementation Details and Additional Results for Few-step Distillation</h2>

<section id="A6.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">F.1 </span>Method and Training Objective</h3>

<div id="A6.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We initialize a student with parameters <math id="A6.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϕ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi</annotation></semantics></math> from the teacher parameters <math id="A6.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math>, and devise a continuous relaxation of Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yin et al. (2024b)</a></cite>) for language models, inspired by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Le Van Kiem et al. (2026)</a></cite> and <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib87" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fan et al. (2026)</a></cite>, to train the student to estimate a clean-context-conditional teacher-generated data distribution <math id="A6.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="p_{\text{teacher}}(\cdot\mid{\mathbf{c}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mtext>teacher</mtext></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mi>𝐜</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{\text{teacher}}(\cdot\mid{\mathbf{c}})</annotation></semantics></math>. In the following we omit the context conditioning for readability.
As detailed in <a href="#A6.SS2" title="F.2 Implementation Details ‣ Appendix F Implementation Details and Additional Results for Few-step Distillation ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F.2</span></a>, this distribution is obtained using the strongest teacher sampler for optimal distributional quality (high NFE and guidance).
We choose <math id="A6.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{\text{teacher}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mtext>teacher</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{\text{teacher}}</annotation></semantics></math> as the target distribution instead of using the pretraining dataset, as we observed that distillation performance was better for the former, likely due to the inductive bias existing in self-distillation since the student is initialized from the teacher.
We ablate this choice along with other design decisions in <a href="#A6.SS3" title="F.3 Additional Results ‣ Appendix F Implementation Details and Additional Results for Few-step Distillation ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F.3</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A6.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We train the student on-policy for a specific number of NFEs <math id="A6.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math>, i.e., the student should produce its own multi-step mapping from the Gaussian prior to the target data distribution by matching intermediate noisy marginals, following the principle in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib87" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fan et al. (2026)</a></cite>.
The training procedure is detailed in <a href="#alg3" title="In F.1 Method and Training Objective ‣ Appendix F Implementation Details and Additional Results for Few-step Distillation ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Alg.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A6.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">At each training iteration,
we pick a clean target sample <math id="A6.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{e}}\sim p_{\text{teacher}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐞</mi><mo>∼</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mtext>teacher</mtext></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{e}}\sim p_{\text{teacher}}</annotation></semantics></math> and independently initialize the rollout with a near-standard-Gaussian state <math id="A6.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{e}}_{1}\sim q_{1}({\mathbf{0}},\gamma_{1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐞</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>∼</mo><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>𝟎</mn><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>γ</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{e}}_{1}\sim q_{1}({\mathbf{0}},\gamma_{1})</annotation></semantics></math>.
The student is rolled out for <math id="A6.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M_{s}\sim\operatorname{Unif}\{0,\dots,M-1\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi>Unif</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M_{s}\sim\operatorname{Unif}\{0,\dots,M-1\}</annotation></semantics></math> steps from <math id="A6.SS1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{e}}_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐞</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{e}}_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> until a <span id="A6.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">source state</span> <math id="A6.SS1.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{e}}_{s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐞</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{e}}_{s}</annotation></semantics></math> with noise level <math id="A6.SS1.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma_{s}=\gamma_{1}-\frac{M_{s}}{M}(\gamma_{1}-\gamma_{0})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>γ</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>γ</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>−</mo><mrow><mfrac><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mi>M</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>γ</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>γ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma_{s}=\gamma_{1}-\frac{M_{s}}{M}(\gamma_{1}-\gamma_{0})</annotation></semantics></math> using self-conditioning.
The multi-step sampler we use for rollout as well as during inference is the consistency-model-style procedure used in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib64" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yin et al. (2024a)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Song et al. (2023)</a></cite>:</p>

<p id="A6.SS1.p3.2" class="ltx_p">This means the intermediate states have the exact same noise marginals as the forward variance-preserving process, but the state is centered around the current clean estimate.
We detach this prefix rollout and treat its source-state distribution as fixed during the selected student update: the student objective is not differentiated through the earlier rollout steps.</p>

<div id="A6.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">From the given source state <math id="A6.SS1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{e}}_{s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐞</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{e}}_{s}</annotation></semantics></math>, the student is called to produce a clean embedding estimate <math id="A6.SS1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{e}}_{0}^{\phi,s}:={\mathbf{e}}_{\phi}({\mathbf{e}}_{s},\gamma_{s})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐞</mi><mn>0</mn><mrow><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo>:=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐞</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐞</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>γ</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{e}}_{0}^{\phi,s}:={\mathbf{e}}_{\phi}({\mathbf{e}}_{s},\gamma_{s})</annotation></semantics></math>, which is re-noised to a <span id="A6.SS1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">query noise level</span> sampled uniformly within the segment starting from the source noise level <math id="A6.SS1.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma_{t}\sim\operatorname{Unif}\Big[\gamma_{1}-\frac{M_{s}+1}{M}(\gamma_{1}-\gamma_{0}),\gamma_{1}-\frac{M_{s}}{M}(\gamma_{1}-\gamma_{0})\Big]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>γ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi>Unif</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.600em" minsize="1.600em">[</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>γ</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>−</mo><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>M</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>γ</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>γ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>γ</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>−</mo><mrow><mfrac><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mi>M</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>γ</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>γ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.600em" minsize="1.600em">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma_{t}\sim\operatorname{Unif}\Big[\gamma_{1}-\frac{M_{s}+1}{M}(\gamma_{1}-\gamma_{0}),\gamma_{1}-\frac{M_{s}}{M}(\gamma_{1}-\gamma_{0})\Big]</annotation></semantics></math>.
This together yields the re-noised student sample <math id="A6.SS1.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{e}}^{\phi,s}_{t}\sim q_{t}({\mathbf{e}}_{0}^{\phi,s}\mid\gamma_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐞</mi><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo>∼</mo><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐞</mi><mn>0</mn><mrow><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><msub><mi>γ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{e}}^{\phi,s}_{t}\sim q_{t}({\mathbf{e}}_{0}^{\phi,s}\mid\gamma_{t})</annotation></semantics></math>
and we denote the resulting marginal as <math id="A6.SS1.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q^{\phi,s}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>q</mi><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q^{\phi,s}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Similarly, the target embedding <math id="A6.SS1.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{e}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐞</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{e}}</annotation></semantics></math> is re-noised to the same query level, yielding a sample <math id="A6.SS1.p4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{e}}_{t}\sim q_{t}({\mathbf{e}},\gamma_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐞</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>∼</mo><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐞</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>γ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{e}}_{t}\sim q_{t}({\mathbf{e}},\gamma_{t})</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A6.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">These choices of source and query distribution correspond to a specific choice of components described in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib87" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fan et al. (2026)</a></cite>.
Like <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib87" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fan et al. (2026)</a></cite>, we train our students in an on-policy fashion; however, we use fully stochastic transitions as in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib64" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yin et al. (2024a)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Le Van Kiem et al. (2026)</a></cite> whereas <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib87" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fan et al. (2026)</a></cite> used deterministic DDIM transitions. Furthermore, we do not use phase experts but only one set of student weights.
As we ablate it later, this specific choice of source and query noise level distributions has a large influence on the overall student quality.</p>
</div>
<div id="A6.SS1.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.SS1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">We match the marginals <math id="A6.SS1.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q^{\phi,s}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>q</mi><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q^{\phi,s}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A6.SS1.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> using reverse-KL, which smooths out the training objective compared to directly trying to match clean embedding distributions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yin et al., 2024b</a>)</cite>:</p>

<p id="A6.SS1.p6.3" class="ltx_p">with <span id="A6.SS1.p6.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">reference denoiser</span> <math id="A6.SS1.p6.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{e}}_{\psi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐞</mi><mi>ψ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{e}}_{\psi}</annotation></semantics></math> (linked to the so-called “real score estimator” in the literature) and the <span id="A6.SS1.p6.3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">auxiliary denoiser</span> <math id="A6.SS1.p6.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{e}}_{\eta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐞</mi><mi>η</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{e}}_{\eta}</annotation></semantics></math> (linked to the “fake score estimator” in the literature).
The full derivation is presented in <a href="#A6.SS4" title="F.4 Proof: DMD Gradient Surrogate Loss ‣ Appendix F Implementation Details and Additional Results for Few-step Distillation ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F.4</span></a>.
The reference denoiser <math id="A6.SS1.p6.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{e}}_{\psi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐞</mi><mi>ψ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{e}}_{\psi}</annotation></semantics></math> denoises the re-noised student’s samples toward the target distribution <math id="A6.SS1.p6.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{\text{teacher}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mtext>teacher</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{\text{teacher}}</annotation></semantics></math>, while the auxiliary denoiser <math id="A6.SS1.p6.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{e}}_{\eta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐞</mi><mi>η</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{e}}_{\eta}</annotation></semantics></math> denoises the re-noised student’s samples toward the student distribution. Steering the student with the detached difference of these two denoisers in <a href="#A6.E19" title="In F.1 Method and Training Objective ‣ Appendix F Implementation Details and Additional Results for Few-step Distillation ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">19</span></a> matches the student and target distributions.
Following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Le Van Kiem et al. (2026)</a></cite>, we train the categorical auxiliary denoiser with a soft-target cross-entropy against the detached student-produced probabilities:</p>

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">

<p id="A6.SS1.p6.4" class="ltx_p">with <math id="A6.SS1.p6.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{e}}_{\eta}={\mathbf{x}}_{\eta}{\mathbf{E}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐞</mi><mi>η</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>η</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐄</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{e}}_{\eta}={\mathbf{x}}_{\eta}{\mathbf{E}}</annotation></semantics></math> .
Usually the teacher diffusion model serves directly as <math id="A6.SS1.p6.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{e}}_{\psi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐞</mi><mi>ψ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{e}}_{\psi}</annotation></semantics></math> since it is trained as a denoiser of the pretraining data distribution <math id="A6.SS1.p6.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{\mathrm{data}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>data</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{\mathrm{data}}</annotation></semantics></math>.
However, since our target distribution is <math id="A6.SS1.p6.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{\text{teacher}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mtext>teacher</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{\text{teacher}}</annotation></semantics></math>, i.e., teacher-generated samples rather than the pretraining distribution, we re-fit the reference denoiser (initialized from the teacher) to <math id="A6.SS1.p6.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{\text{teacher}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mtext>teacher</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{\text{teacher}}</annotation></semantics></math> using cross-entropy:</p>

<div id="A6.SS1.p7" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.SS1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">The auxiliary denoiser, the reference denoiser and the main student all use same-state two-call training for self-conditioning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2023</a>)</cite> with probability <math id="A6.SS1.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{\text{SC}}=0.25" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mtext>SC</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.25</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{\text{SC}}=0.25</annotation></semantics></math> while inference carries the previous raw clean prediction, thereby mimicking the original teacher’s training and inference behaviors.
The complete training procedure is summarized in <a href="#alg3" title="In F.1 Method and Training Objective ‣ Appendix F Implementation Details and Additional Results for Few-step Distillation ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Alg.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A6.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">F.2 </span>Implementation Details</h3>

<section id="A6.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Target distribution.</h5>

<div id="A6.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The target distribution is a teacher-generated bank
containing 65,536 clean prefixes of 256 tokens, taken from the pretraining dataset,
and four teacher-generated
32-token continuation blocks per prefix.
This bank is generated with the empirically optimal teacher sampler, i.e.,
256-step DDPM sampling with self-conditioning enabled and optimal guidance: for <span id="A6.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span>-3B this is CFG <math id="A6.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w=2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w=2</annotation></semantics></math> and ST <math id="A6.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau=0.1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau=0.1</annotation></semantics></math>, whereas for <span id="A6.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span>-8B this is CFG <math id="A6.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w=3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w=3</annotation></semantics></math> and ST <math id="A6.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau=0.1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau=0.1</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A6.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Parameterization and optimization.</h5>

<div id="A6.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">All three neural networks are initialized from the same respective teacher checkpoint,
with separate trainable parameter copies and optimizers. We copy the embedding matrix, noise schedule and noise endpoints from the teacher and retain them throughout
distillation.
We detach the source rollout and the SC preliminary
prediction, so student gradients pass only through the selected
denoising transition, similar to <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib87" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fan et al. (2026)</a></cite>.
We prefit the reference denoiser <math id="A6.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbf{e}}_{\psi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐞</mi><mi>ψ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbf{e}}_{\psi}</annotation></semantics></math> for 50 optimizer updates before starting student/auxiliary updates. Each subsequent student update is preceded by four auxiliary updates
and four reference updates.
We optimize all networks with AdamW with a global batch size of 256, <math id="A6.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta_{1}=0.9" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>β</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.9</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta_{1}=0.9</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A6.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta_{2}=0.999" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>β</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.999</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta_{2}=0.999</annotation></semantics></math>, zero
weight decay, and unit-norm gradient clipping. The learning rates for each network are selected through gradient balancing and are <math id="A6.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3.6\times 10^{-7}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>3.6</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3.6\times 10^{-7}</annotation></semantics></math> for the student,
<math id="A6.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1.188\times 10^{-5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.188</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.188\times 10^{-5}</annotation></semantics></math> for the auxiliary denoiser, and <math id="A6.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10^{-6}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10^{-6}</annotation></semantics></math> for the reference denoiser.</p>
</div>
<div id="A6.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In practice, we use the residual-normalization strategy in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib64" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yin et al. (2024a)</a></cite> and remove the SNR weight <math id="A6.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathrm{e}}^{-\gamma_{t}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>γ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathrm{e}}^{-\gamma_{t}}</annotation></semantics></math>, thereby replacing <a href="#A6.E19" title="In F.1 Method and Training Objective ‣ Appendix F Implementation Details and Additional Results for Few-step Distillation ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">19</span></a> with</p>

<p id="A6.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.2" class="ltx_p">with the student-to-reference denoiser residual</p>

<section id="A6.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">F.3 </span>Additional Results</h3>

<section id="A6.SS3.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Diversity and pass@<math id="A6.SS3.SSS0.Px1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>.</h5>

<div id="A6.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We demonstrate here that our distribution-matching distillation procedure preserves the diversity of the target teacher distribution, i.e., we do not fall into the pitfall often encountered in DMD methods.
We use 512 prompts and sample 8 trajectories per prompt, on 3 benchmarks (GSM8K, MBPP and Novelty-Bench).
GSM8K measures math reasoning, MBPP measures coding ability, and Novelty-Bench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib88" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2025</a>)</cite> is an open-ended creative writing benchmark which helps us measure actual text diversity and creativity.</p>
</div>
<div id="A6.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We measure pass@<math id="A6.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math> and pass@<math id="A6.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>8</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">8</annotation></semantics></math> accuracies as well as semantic diversity using the Vendi score <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib89" title="" class="ltx_ref">Friedman and Dieng, 2023</a>)</cite>. We compute the Vendi score as the exponentiated Jensen-Shannon entropy of the pairwise similarity matrix between SentenceBERT embeddings of the produced outputs.
Results displayed in
<a href="#A6.F20" title="In Diversity and pass@𝑘. ‣ F.3 Additional Results ‣ Appendix F Implementation Details and Additional Results for Few-step Distillation ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figs.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">20</span></a>, <a href="#A6.F21" title="Figure 21 ‣ Diversity and pass@𝑘. ‣ F.3 Additional Results ‣ Appendix F Implementation Details and Additional Results for Few-step Distillation ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">21</span></a> and <a href="#A6.F22" title="Figure 22 ‣ Diversity and pass@𝑘. ‣ F.3 Additional Results ‣ Appendix F Implementation Details and Additional Results for Few-step Distillation ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">22</span></a>
clearly demonstrate that our DMD student recovers the DDPM-256 Vendi score as well as its pass@<math id="A6.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>8</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">8</annotation></semantics></math> accuracy, with as few as 4 diffusion steps. Furthermore, the DDIM-32 <span id="A6.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span>-3B (with self-conditioning) teacher has lower diversity and pass@<math id="A6.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>8</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">8</annotation></semantics></math> accuracy than both our <span id="A6.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span> -<span id="A6.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">distill</span>-3B students and the DDPM-256 <span id="A6.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span>-3B, although its pass@<math id="A6.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math> is somewhat comparable to our 4-NFE <span id="A6.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span> -<span id="A6.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">distill</span>-3B.
This suggests that our distilled students balance quality and diversity for only a fraction of the inference cost, which is very promising for, e.g., RL-based post-training.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A6.F20" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2610.02665v2/fig20_diversity_gsm8k.svg" id="A6.F20.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:381/152;" width="381" height="152"></object>

</figure>

</figure>

<section id="A6.SS3.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Ablation 1: Teacher.</h5>

<div id="A6.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We investigate the influence of the teacher’s geometry on the distillation performance. We observed earlier that improving the regularity of the geometry is key for low-NFE performance. Indeed, the unregularized <span id="A6.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span> -<span id="A6.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">unreg</span>-3B teacher exhibits local embedding collapse, lowering the global rank participation and creating uncertainty during decoding, which particularly affects coding tasks (see <a href="#S4.SS3" title="4.3 Embedding Regularization ‣ 4 Language Generation via Continuous Diffusion Sampling ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Secs.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.3</span></a> and <a href="#A5.T10" title="Table 10 ‣ Appendix E Implementation Details and Additional Results for Inference ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>).
This consequence transfers naturally to the distillation quality, as we notice in <a href="#A6.F23" title="In Ablation 1: Teacher. ‣ F.3 Additional Results ‣ Appendix F Implementation Details and Additional Results for Few-step Distillation ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">23</span></a> that <span id="A6.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span>-3B teaches much stronger students at 4- and 8-NFE in particular.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A6.F23" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2610.02665v2/fig23_teacher_ablation.svg" id="A6.F23.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:381/151;" width="381" height="151"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A6.F23.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 23</span>: </span><span id="A6.F23.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Teacher ablation for DMD distillation at 3B scale. Global batch size 64.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="A6.SS3.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Ablation 2: Global Batch Size.</h5>

<div id="A6.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We ablate the effect of global batch size on distillation quality. Increasing the global batch size from 64 to 256 yields large and consistent improvements across NFEs. Increasing batch size above 256 did not further improve results.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A6.F24" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2610.02665v2/fig24_batch_size.svg" id="A6.F24.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:381/148;" width="381" height="148"></object>

</figure>
</section>
<section id="A6.SS3.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Ablation 3: Query Distributions.</h5>

<div id="A6.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Choosing the query distribution is a key design choice in DMD distillation. After obtaining very good early results with Phased DMD <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib87" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fan et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, we ablated the discrepancies between Phased DMD and plain DMD, and noticed that the source states, the transitions and the source and query distributions were the most discriminative factors. As we kept the consistency-style transitions with fresh Gaussian noise and the student rollout for obtaining our input states, the main remaining difference was the query distribution.
We choose three candidate distributions: Uniform, Gumbel fitted to the teacher’s empirical denoising cross-entropy distribution (skewed toward intermediate noise levels), and <math id="A6.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta(2.5,1)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2.5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta(2.5,1)</annotation></semantics></math> (skewed toward high noise levels); as well as three ranges for the distribution support: the whole range <math id="A6.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[\gamma_{0},\gamma_{1}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><msub><mi>γ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>γ</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[\gamma_{0},\gamma_{1}]</annotation></semantics></math>, within segment <math id="A6.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[\gamma_{r},\gamma_{t}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><msub><mi>γ</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>γ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[\gamma_{r},\gamma_{t}]</annotation></semantics></math>, and above segment <math id="A6.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[\gamma_{t},\gamma_{1}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><msub><mi>γ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>γ</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[\gamma_{t},\gamma_{1}]</annotation></semantics></math>.
We conduct this ablation specifically on the 4-NFE distillation setup.
In <a href="#A6.F25" title="In Ablation 3: Query Distributions. ‣ F.3 Additional Results ‣ Appendix F Implementation Details and Additional Results for Few-step Distillation ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">25</span></a>, we observe that using the current segment as the support consistently obtained the best results, and that the exact distribution did not matter so much there. The teacher-CE-fit Gumbel above segment obtained excellent results too, but we noticed that the resulting distillation procedure was very unstable.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A6.F25" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2610.02665v2/fig25_query_distribution.svg" id="A6.F25.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:381/148;" width="381" height="148"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A6.F25.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 25</span>: </span><span id="A6.F25.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Query distribution ablation for DMD distillation from <span id="A6.F25.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span>-3B teacher. Global batch size 64. <math id="A6.F25.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M=4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M=4</annotation></semantics></math> NFE distillation.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="A6.SS3.SSS0.Px5" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Ablation 4: Self-conditioning and student input.</h5>

<div id="A6.SS3.SSS0.Px5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.SS3.SSS0.Px5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Using self-conditioning in the student is absolutely key to its generation quality.
The self-conditioning probability used during distillation hardly influences the result: for simplicity we retain <math id="A6.SS3.SSS0.Px5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{\text{SC}}=0.25" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mtext>SC</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.25</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{\text{SC}}=0.25</annotation></semantics></math>.
Using <math id="A6.SS3.SSS0.Px5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{\text{SC}}=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mtext>SC</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{\text{SC}}=0</annotation></semantics></math> degraded results slightly, but far worse is deactivating self-conditioning at inference, as shown in <a href="#A6.F26" title="In Ablation 4: Self-conditioning and student input. ‣ F.3 Additional Results ‣ Appendix F Implementation Details and Additional Results for Few-step Distillation ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">26</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A6.F26" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2610.02665v2/fig26_self_conditioning.svg" id="A6.F26.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:381/148;" width="381" height="148"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A6.F26.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 26</span>: </span><span id="A6.F26.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Self-conditioning ablation for DMD distillation from <span id="A6.F26.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span>-3B teacher. Global batch size 64.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="A6.SS3.SSS0.Px6" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Ablation 5: Training data.</h5>

<div id="A6.SS3.SSS0.Px6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.SS3.SSS0.Px6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We observe in <a href="#A6.F27" title="In Ablation 5: Training data. ‣ F.3 Additional Results ‣ Appendix F Implementation Details and Additional Results for Few-step Distillation ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">27</span></a> that teacher-generated data led to better results than directly using the pretraining dataset. We posit this is due to the inductive bias carried by the student about the target distribution, since it is initialized from the teacher that produced this distribution.
We conduct this ablation specifically on the 4-NFE distillation setup.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A6.F27" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2610.02665v2/fig27_training_data.svg" id="A6.F27.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:381/149;" width="381" height="149"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A6.F27.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 27</span>: </span><span id="A6.F27.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Data distribution ablation for DMD distillation from <span id="A6.F27.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span>-3B teacher. Global batch size 64. <math id="A6.F27.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M=4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M=4</annotation></semantics></math> NFE distillation.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="A6.SS3.SSS0.Px7" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Ablation 6: Student and auxiliary objectives.</h5>

<div id="A6.SS3.SSS0.Px7.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.SS3.SSS0.Px7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We ablate the choice of student loss weighting (“Norm off SNR on” <a href="#A6.E19" title="In F.1 Method and Training Objective ‣ Appendix F Implementation Details and Additional Results for Few-step Distillation ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">19</span></a> vs. “Norm on SNR off” <a href="#A6.E22" title="In Parameterization and optimization. ‣ F.2 Implementation Details ‣ Appendix F Implementation Details and Additional Results for Few-step Distillation ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">22</span></a>) and the auxiliary denoiser parameterization and objective.
“Soft CE” indicates our baseline, i.e., a categorical denoiser (similar to the teacher) trained with cross-entropy on soft probabilities. “MSE” indicates a denoiser augmented with an MLP-parameterized residual connection from Transformer final hidden state to the re-embedded categorical prediction, trained with MSE in the embedding space directly.
We conduct this ablation specifically on the 4-NFE distillation setup.
The results highlighted in <a href="#A6.F28" title="In Ablation 6: Student and auxiliary objectives. ‣ F.3 Additional Results ‣ Appendix F Implementation Details and Additional Results for Few-step Distillation ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">28</span></a> favor the Soft CE auxiliary objective introduced in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Le Van Kiem et al. (2026)</a></cite>; the DMD2-type normalization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib64" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yin et al., 2024a</a>)</cite> does not play a major role, although we informally observed it led to faster and more stable convergence, therefore being favored in our final setup.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A6.F28" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2610.02665v2/fig28_student_objective.svg" id="A6.F28.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:381/152;" width="381" height="152"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A6.F28.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 28</span>: </span><span id="A6.F28.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Student objective ablation for DMD distillation from <span id="A6.F28.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sigma</span>-3B teacher. Global batch size 64. <math id="A6.F28.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M=4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M=4</annotation></semantics></math> NFE distillation.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>

<section id="A6.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">F.4 </span>Proof: DMD Gradient Surrogate Loss</h3>

<div id="A6.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we prove the form of the DMD gradient surrogate loss in <a href="#A6.E19" title="In F.1 Method and Training Objective ‣ Appendix F Implementation Details and Additional Results for Few-step Distillation ‣ Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">19</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A6.SS4.2" class="ltx_proof">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_font_italic ltx_title_proof">Proof.</h6>
<div id="A6.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A6.SS4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text">We first fix the source and query noise levels <math id="A6.SS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\gamma_{s},\gamma_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>γ</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>γ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\gamma_{s},\gamma_{t})</annotation></semantics></math>.
All distributions below are implicitly conditioned on the clean prefix.
For this derivation, we hold the source-state sampling distribution
fixed, consistently with detaching the on-policy source rollout.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="A6.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A6.SS4.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text">Write <math id="A6.SS4.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha_{t}=\alpha(\gamma_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>α</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>γ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha_{t}=\alpha(\gamma_{t})</annotation></semantics></math> and
<math id="A6.SS4.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{t}=\sigma(\gamma_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>γ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{t}=\sigma(\gamma_{t})</annotation></semantics></math>.
The Gaussian corruption admits the reparameterization</span></p>
